Antarctica is a key region for carbon cycling and export. The efficiency of carbon export has been linked to the type of phytoplankton dominating the system. Our results suggest diatoms, haptophytes, and cryptophytes are present in all water column samples despite substantial physical differences between sampling locations. Our data shows a strong relationship between the proportion of diatoms, haptophytes, and cryptophytes relative to all other phytoplankton and the magnitude of carbon flux.

title: The Global Phosphorylation Landscape of Acute Heat Stress in Reef-Building Corals
content: Warming oceans disrupt the coral-algal symbiosis that sustains reefs, yet the signaling mechanisms initiating bleaching remain poorly understood. Integrating global phosphoproteomics across three reef-building corals with protein structure modeling revealed conservation between coral and human kinases, enabling inference of coral kinase activities and uncovering a shared signaling program induced by acute heat stress. Heat rapidly activated ERK, JNK, and p38 MAP kinases, suppressed cell cycle signaling, and remodeled pathways controlling chromatin, RNA processing, and metabolism. Most strikingly, thermal stress rewired immune receptor signaling networks associated with non-self recognition, suggesting that heat shifts the coral host from tolerance to immune recognition of its algal symbionts. These findings define conserved signaling mechanisms that precede bleaching, revealing actionable molecular targets for enhancing coral resilience.

title: Uncovering disease progression trajectories across multiple timescales with hybrid ODE-mixture models
content: Biological systems are capable of evolving across multiple timescales, yet most modeling approaches capture either short-term physiological responses or long-term disease progression. Additionally, methods that combine these time scales either struggle with inter-individual variation, or require large volumes of data to work. We present Latent Class Parameter Trajectory Analysis (LCPTA), a hybrid framework that combines mechanistic ordinary differential equation (ODE) modeling of short-term dynamics with latent class trajectory modeling of long-term parameter evolution. To support this approach, we developed TemporalMixtureModels.jl, a Julia package for univariate and multivariate temporal mixture modeling. We evaluated LCPTA in two synthetic longitudinal studies, covering a simulation of a heterogeneous population developing hypertension, as well as a synthetic longitudinal study of 75 virtual individuals followed over 30 years, representing muscle insulin resistance, liver insulin resistance, and healthy trajectories. We compared LCPTA with a conditional neural ODE and a conditional neural network for reconstruction of long-term parameter trajectories and subgroup separation. In both studies LCPTA recovered relevant subgroup structure and trajectory patterns. In the cardiovascular study, the neural approaches were able to distinguish inter-individual differences, but in the insulin sensitivity study, neural approaches failed to represent parameter trajectories faithfully, primarily separating individuals along a single dominant parameter and showing weaker multivariate trajectory reconstruction. In additional experiments with sparse and irregularly sampled unseen individuals, LCPTA maintained strong classification performance. We show that LCPTA is an efficient and interpretable strategy for multiscale modeling of heterogeneous metabolic disease progression, with potential utility for data-efficient digital twin applications.

title: Characterisation of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces jurei hybrids for oenological applications
content: The Saccharomyces genus present as a genetically diverse set of microorganisms capable of tolerating a range of environmental stressors, demonstrating high fermentation capacity and producing interesting flavour compounds. Such diversity can be exploited in a single organism by producing interspecies hybrids, overcoming the limitations of a single species. Here, as proof of principle, we exploited a library of F12 interspecies diploid hybrids between Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces jurei (Sc/Sj), to identify new strains harbouring traits of oenological relevance, such as ethanol and glycerol production, superior tolerance to acetic acid, limited production of H2S, and optimal growth on fructose. Moreover, we calculated robustness across strains tested on solid media comparing the trade-off between performance on a single conditions and overall robustness. Progeny from a range of robustness values with favourable H2S production profiles were isolated for further analysis via micro and small-scale fermentations. Micro-scale fermentations in synthetic grape must containing individual wine-associated stressors were performed, and the robustness of the selected strains was confirmed. The wine characteristics of the hybrids were tested in small-scale fermentations in synthetic grape media. We found that both ethanol and glycerol production across our selected progeny matched or exceeding that from the commercial wine strain, and most hybrids produced less acetic acid and more fatty-acids, including higher quantities of associated esters. Overall, we were able to identify suitable Sc/Sj hybrids with interesting aroma profiles to develop further for wine fermentation.

title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya and related parahenipaviruses
content: Langya virus is a zoonotic parahenipavirus with pandemic potential that causes acute febrile illness in people. We identified endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) as an entry receptor for Langya, Wenzhou, and Mojiang parahenipaviruses. A 3.1 [A] cryo-electron microscopy structure reveals that Langya attachment glycoprotein engages EPCR through a site distinct from that of the ephrin binding site of Nipah G. This binding mode resembles those of protein C and a malarial adhesin, demonstrating convergent evolution. Interface substitutions abolish entry, whereas natural variation explains differential human EPCR use and predicts receptor compatibility across 26 animal species. These findings establish EPCR as a receptor for the Langya clade and provide a structural framework for understanding cross-species transmission and human infection potential.

title: Cross-regulatory sRNA networks shape adaptive stress responses in Staphylococcus aureus: RsaC and RsaOI regulate galactose metabolism and cell wall homeostasis
content: Staphylococcus aureus is a major human pathogen whose adaptability relies on network of regulators, including two-component systems, transcription factors and small regulatory RNAs. Yet most of these regulators are dispensable for growth, suggesting cooperation or redundancy between them. To explore this hypothesis, we performed a yeast one-hybrid screen of 43 TFs against the promoters of seven sRNAs, which identified 27 novel TF-sRNA promoter interactions. We then focused on three sRNAs. We showed that srn_9342 is repressed by VraR and MntR, which also control rsaOI and rsaC, respectively. We found that rsaC, like rsaOI, is induced by acidic pH and vancomycin exposure, whereas srn_9342 expression remained unchanged. We also demonstrated in vitro that Srn_9342 interacts with both RsaOI and RsaC. Its role toward these two sRNAs remains unknown, but this interaction raises the possibility that it modulates their availability or activity. RsaOI and RsaC both act on the tagatose pathway for galactose utilization, through different genes: lacD for RsaOI, as previously reported, and lacC for RsaC, newly identified here. We showed that both sRNAs are required for surface charge remodeling and for growth under subinhibitory vancomycin. They also modulate the virulence factors PSM and protein A. Both sRNAs reduce PSM production, whereas protein A is decreased by RsaOI, likely through Rot, and increased by RsaC through an unknown, probably indirect mechanism. Together, our results suggest that a single cell wall stress can engage several regulators that could cooperate on shared targets or pathways, which may explain why individual regulators are dispensable.

title: Tripartite toxin-antitoxin system regulates the production and release of pneumolysin by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
content: The production of toxins is critical to the success of bacteria, with their targets and outcomes varying widely. Pneumolysin (Ply), produced by the major human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae, is a cytolytic pore forming toxin that plays many diverse roles including inducing tissue damage and inflammation, evasion of many aspects of the human immune system, invasion of the bacteria into deeper tissue, and transmission to new hosts. Despite its importance, many aspects of the biology of this toxin have to date remained unknown, in particular, what role of the three other genes that form part of the ply operon play in Ply production. Here we demonstrate that these genes encode a complex regulatory system, that includes a putative membrane destabilising protein (PlyA) and a MazEF-like toxin-antitoxin system (PlyB and PlyC), the toxin of which (PlyC) destabilises the Ply transcript. We propose a tripartite model whereby when the operon reaches relatively high levels of expression PlyA destabilises the S. pneumoniae membrane creating a stress that triggers a necessary negative feedback loop which results in the degradation of the PlyB antitoxin, release of the PlyC toxin and degradation of the ply transcript, thereby providing a means by which Ply production can be tightly regulated. Given the importance of Ply to the ability of S. pneumoniae to cause infection, identifying the factors that result in the shutdown of Ply production and release by the bacteria would seem promising target for future therapeutic strategies.

title: Butyrate reverts Chlamydia pneumoniae -induced transcriptional suppression of macrophage polarization markers and promotes chlamydial clearance in macrophages
content: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are generated by gut microbiota through fermentation of dietary fibers. SCFAs contribute to human health through immunomodulation, metabolic regulation and other extra intestinal functions. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of SCFAs on the survival and antibiotic susceptibility of the intracellular bacteria Chlamydia pneumoniae and Chlamydia trachomatis, both representing prevalent human pathogens associated with chronic sequelae. Despite earlier reports on their direct antimicrobial activity, none of the three major SCFAs acetate, propionate nor butyrate affected the growth of C. pneumoniae or C. trachomatis in epithelial cells. However, butyrate decreased C. pneumoniae genome copy numbers and infectious progeny production in THP-1 macrophages harbouring antibiotic-refractory infection phenotype. In addition, butyrate enhanced the chlamydiocidal efficacy of azithromycin in the macrophages. Similar results were obtained with C. trachomatis-infected macrophages. To elucidate the underlying molecular changes, impact of chlamydial infection, butyrate treatment and the combination theirof on macrophage polarization and antimicrobial peptide expression was investigated. C. pneumoniae suppressed the expression of macrophage polarization markers CD80, TLR4, CD64, CD204 and CD206, and the antimicrobial peptide LL37, while butyrate treatment reverted the expression of both the polarization markers and LL37 in the infected macrophages. These findings suggest that butyrate may play a role in modulating immune responses in macrophages during Chlamydia infections, highlighting the role of diet-derived metabolites in shaping Chlamydia-host interactions and antichlamydial treatment efficacy.

title: Age Associated Shifts Toward Anaerobic Taxa and Amino Acid Degradation Potential in the Canine Oral Microbiome
content: Introduction: Periodontal disease is common in dogs and is associated with changes in oral microbial community composition. How the canine oral microbiome restructures across age at both ecological and metabolic levels remains incompletely characterized. Methods: We analyzed shotgun metagenomic buccal-swab profiles from 1,125 dogs using MetaPhlAn. Functional profiles from HUMAnN were analyzed at pathway and functional-group levels. We annotated species-level taxa with oxygen preference and evaluated oxygen-tolerant and anaerobic taxa abundances across age. We also characterized community structure, metabolic potential, Shannon diversity, and age and weight prediction using nested cross-validated Elastic Net models. Results: Age was associated with substantial restructuring in the oral microbiome. Mean oxygen-tolerant taxa abundance decreased from 67.5% in puppies to 29.1% in mature dogs, whereas anaerobic abundance increased from 14.3% to 53.8%. The oxygen-tolerant: anaerobe log-ratio declined with age (Spearman {rho} = -0.616). Metabolic profiles also varied with age, with higher amino-acid-degradation potential and lower glycolysis and central-carbohydrate potential, and aerobic-respiration-I abundance in older dogs. Shannon diversity increased with age ({rho} = 0.537, p < 0.001). Elastic Net models trained on microbiome species abundance predicted age (Pearson r = 0.609; R-squared = 0.371) and weight (r = 0.498; R-squared = 0.248) with moderate accuracy. Discussion: Canine age was associated with coordinated changes in oral-community oxygen preference and metabolic pathways. These findings extend prior taxon-specific observations by examining a broader ecological shift and metabolic potential in the canine oral microbiome. This provides a reference for future longitudinal or clinical studies of oral maturation and periodontal disease.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encoding CagW, a conserved component of the Helicobacter pylori type IV secretion system, protects mice against H. pylori challenge
content: Background: Roughly one person in two carries Helicobacter pylori, a pathogen classified by the World Health Organization as a group I carcinogen, and the steady loss of antibiotic efficacy has made prophylaxis an urgent rather than an optional goal. No mRNA vaccine against this organism has yet been tested in the clinic, and CagW, a conserved inner-membrane subunit of the H. pylori type IV secretion system (T4SS), has never been evaluated as an mRNA-encoded antigen. Methods: A codon-optimised construct carrying a signal peptide, the CagW coding sequence and a human IgG Fc tag was synthesised, transcribed into mRNA, encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and shown to direct antigen expression in HEK293T cells. C57BL/6 mice received three intramuscular doses of CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs (5 ug mRNA each) at 14-day intervals; animals given alum alone, luciferase mRNA-LNPs or CagW protein adsorbed to alum served as comparators. Humoral readouts (IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, IgM, IgA and secretory IgA), lymphocyte proliferation, CD4+/CD8+ subsets, intracellular IFN-{gamma}, IL-4 and IL-17A and circulating cytokines were quantified before challenge, and protection was assessed after live challenge. Results: The formulation (93.2 nm; PDI 0.13; approximately 90% encapsulation) produced CagW-specific protein in vitro. Vaccination raised high-titre CagW-specific IgG (maximal on day 42), IgM and mucosal sIgA, and drove Th1/Th2-type cellular activation (IL-2, IL-4, IL-12, IFN-{gamma} and IL-17A). After challenge, immunised animals carried markedly fewer gastric bacteria and showed lower urease activity than controls. Conclusions: CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs are therefore a credible mRNA vaccine platform for H. pylori and warrant further preclinical development.

title: Experimental evolution reveals temporally opposing roles for Csu pili during Acinetobacter baumannii respiratory infection
content: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen responsible for a wide range of infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and urinary tract infections. Most studies investigating A. baumannii pulmonary pathogenesis rely on acute pneumonia models that use high bacterial inocula and do not recapitulate the prolonged infections observed in some patients. Recently, our laboratory developed a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection that enabled the identification of virulence factors specifically required for long-term lung persistence. To investigate how A. baumannii adapts during chronic pulmonary infection, we performed an experimental evolution study using this model. This approach revealed an unexpected role for the archaic chaperone-usher (Csu) pili in A. baumannii pathogenesis. At early time points, Csu expression reduced bacterial burdens in both acute and chronic pneumonia models, an effect associated with enhanced host inflammatory responses. In contrast, at later stages of chronic infection, Csu promoted bacterial persistence, potentially by facilitating adhesion to pulmonary epithelial cells. These opposing effects were conserved across two distinct A. baumannii clinical isolates. We also found that Csu contributes to bacterial colonization in a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) model in a strain-dependent manner. Together, these findings reveal an infection-stage-dependent role for Csu in A. baumannii pathogenesis, demonstrating that a bacterial surface structure can impair early colonization while promoting long-term persistence.

title: A Vma13-targeted thiadiazole-succinimide disrupts V-ATPase dependent arginine-polyamine homeostasis to block Candida albicans escape from macrophages
content: Invasive candidiasis caused by Candida albicans is a life-threatening nosocomial infection with limited therapies and high morbidity and mortality among immunocompromised patients. Within host phagocytes, C. albicans catabolizes arginine to produce ammonia and fuels polyamine biosynthesis, which correlates with phagosomal alkalinization and yeast-to-hypha morphogenesis, facilitating macrophage escape and systemic dissemination. However, new antifungal strategies blocking this fungal escape remain scarce. Here, we characterize the thiadiazole-succinimide derivative ETSI, an arginine-dependent antifungal small molecule with minimal direct growth inhibition under arginine-free conditions yet robust anti-C. albicans activity in arginine-rich microenvironments mimicking the macrophage intracellular niche. Mechanistically, ETSI targets the vacuolar Vma13 to inhibit vacuolar H-ATPase (V-ATPase), dissipating vacuolar proton (H+) gradients and leading to cytoplasmic H+ retention. The accumulated cytoplasmic H+ traps intracellular ammonia and blocks its external release, while impaired vacuolar metabolite sequestration further triggers cytotoxic accumulation of arginine and polyamine metabolites. This dual metabolic perturbation suppresses phagosomal alkalinization, retains C. albicans in yeast form and blocks macrophage escape. ETSI is the first small molecule blocking C. albicans escape via disrupted Vma13/V-ATPase dependent arginine-polyamine homeostasis. This work identifies an intracellular metabolic vulnerability and establishes a niche-targeted antifungal strategy distinct from classic growth-suppressive drugs for treating invasive candidiasis.

title: Identifying the source population of naturally recolonised rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) in Laokhowa-Burhachapori Wildlife Sanctuary, Assam, through multidisciplinary methods
content: Megaherbivore population recovery largely depends on restoring connectivity between fragmented protected areas to facilitate natural dispersal, gene flow, and range expansion. The Indian rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) has recovered from severe population decline in the past, but several populations remain spatially restricted. Recent conservation efforts and the expansion of protected areas in Assam have coincided with natural rhino recolonization in Laokhowa-Burhachapori Wildlife Sanctuary (WLS). This has occurred from nearby regions of Orang NP and Kaziranga NP after the species was locally extinct in the 1980s. Identifying the source population of these recolonised rhinos is crucial for managing this emerging metapopulation. We used non-invasive genetic sampling, genetic assignment and a landscape connectivity model to investigate the origin and potential movement routes of the recolonising rhinos. We identified eight unique individuals from Laokhowa-Burhachapori WLS and assigned them to the potential source population using Bayesian and frequency-based approaches against a reference dataset of 365 individual rhinos across the rhino-bearing areas of Assam. Habitat suitability was modelled using 161 spatially thinned presence points and eight environmental variables. We applied least-cost path (LCP) analysis to assess landscape resistance between protected area nodes. All eight recolonising rhinos were assigned to Orang NP with high Bayesian assignment probabilities (q = 0.97-0.99). The connectivity model identified two least-cost pathways, with the Orang NP-Laokhowa-Burhachapori WLS linkage showing lower landscape friction than the Kaziranga NP linkage. These findings provide genetic evidence that the recolonisation occurred through natural dispersal, most likely from Orang NP, and indicate that recent landscape restoration has re-established the structural connectivity across this floodplain. Maintaining these linkages will be essential to promote natural range expansion and the long-term persistence of Indian rhinoceros in Assam.

title: Tropical Peatlands as Hotspots of Hidden Arcellinida Diversity: Insights from Maludam National Park, Borneo (Sarawak, Malaysia)
content: Recent investigations on tropical peatlands have shown their extremely high efficiency as carbon sinks, far beyond better studied boreal bogs. The microbial diversity found in those ecosystems, as well as their corresponding ecological and metabolic processes, are just starting to be revealed, and differ considerably from high latitudes systems. However, these efforts have been concentrated almost exclusively towards prokaryotes and fungi, leaving protist communities virtually unknown. Arcellinida (testate amoebae) are well acknowledged to play an important role in boreal and temperate peatland ecology by driving microbial community composition as top predators, but also as nutrient recyclers and carbon fixers. Yet, to our knowledge, no community-level study has addressed their diversity and its drivers in tropical peatlands. In this study, we surveyed Arcellinida communities' diversity across five functionally distinct vegetation-hydrological zones situated along a hydrological transect in a coastal tropical peatland in the Maludam National Park, Malaysia. Taxonomic composition of Arcellinida communities, characterized by a high diversity of Trigonopyxis-related taxa, indicated fundamental differences in diversity and community composition from extratropical ecosystems. Species richness was significantly higher in the zones with developed understory vegetation. Furthermore, the composition of diversity varied significantly among vegetation-hydrological zones. Altogether, this study shows unique Arcellinida communities in a Southeastern Asian peatland and suggests the importance of vegetation-hydrological characteristics for protist diversity.

title: Harmonizing Repeated Multi-Platform Optical and LiDAR Observations for Continental-Scale Terrestrial Carbon Cycle Data Assimilation.
content: Accurate monitoring of terrestrial carbon has attracted considerable attention due to the impacts of rapid climate change, disturbance, and land use on carbon storage and the growth of new global carbon markets and reporting requirements. While uncertainties in C estimates remain nontrivial, crucial opportunities exist to reduce uncertainty by rigorously harmonizing models and monitoring through data assimilation (DA). LiDAR has received considerable attention for its potential to inform carbon monitoring, and while there have been a number of papers on how to initialize models using LiDAR data, it has yet to be integrated into DA systems. In this study, we integrate GEDI LiDAR into an established DA system that already assimilates optical observations of aboveground biomass (AGB) and leaf area index (LAI), microwave soil moisture (SM), and ground-based soil organic carbon (SOC) to constrain C cycling processes across the entire North American continent. Notably, this is the first time both optical and LiDAR AGB products have been iteratively harmonized within a DA system. Results show that by assimilating both optical and LiDAR observations, we reduced the uncertainty in woody biomass by 63.7% relative to unconstrained model simulations and 18% relative to our previous DA system, and achieved an average RMSE reduction of 38.3 kg/m2 across five AGB products. Importantly, LiDAR reduces DA biases in high AGB regions where optical AGB estimates were exhibiting saturation. Analysis further identified the leading factors driving spatial error patterns within the DA system to be data quality, cloud coverage, and elevation. Overall, by bridging the spatial and temporal limitations of individual satellite products, this approach offers a practical, generalized workflow for high-resolution terrestrial carbon MRV in complex, dynamic ecosystems.

title: Ancient environmental DNA reveals the distinct fingerprints of whaling and climate change on Antarctic marine biodiversity
content: The Southern Ocean is a disproportionately large contributor to Earth system processes, playing a crucial role in the global transport of carbon, oxygen and heat. It also hosts enormous seasonal biological productivity that supports diverse endemic marine biodiversity. Industrial whaling in the first half of the 20th century and recent human-driven climate change have both profoundly altered Antarctic ecosystems, but ecological surveys of these impacts are limited to well-known taxa in the short period since monitoring began. Here, we analysed five sediment records to reconstruct more than two centuries of ecosystem change across the Western Antarctic Peninsula, spanning periods before and during major human impacts. Environmental DNA metabarcoding of these records revealed substantial biodiversity shifts, with change accelerating in recent decades. We find a significant role for both climate change and whaling in restructuring communities, identifying unique variance in whole-community change explained by each driver. Moreover, we find a negative association between whaling and metazoan families which feed from the water column, suggesting that pre-whaling ecosystems had greater pelagic productivity. Overall, our results reveal baseline Antarctic biodiversity from long before observational records and identify a distinct fingerprint of human drivers in this fragile, rapidly changing ecosystem.

title: MillionTrees: A global benchmark for tree detection across geography, sensor, and annotation geometry
content: Airborne tree monitoring using remotely sensed data, combined with the growth of computer vision models for object detection and segmentation, can facilitate broad scale assessment of tree health, ecology and ecosystem function. However, datasets for airborne tree detection have been largely limited to a single geography, resolution, or annotation approach, making it difficult to develop general models and benchmark their utility for broad applications. We compile existing and newly published annotation datasets to create a comprehensive dataset for training and evaluating airborne tree detection in RGB imagery. The MillionTrees dataset has over a million individual trees from a broad range of forest types, tree species, and geographic locations. In addition, it has six million weakly supervised annotations from a range of sources including airborne LiDAR and photogrammetry, arborist surveys, and simulated landscapes. An evaluation standard is provided to facilitate rapid model development. We benchmark several existing tree detection algorithms and demonstrate that while current open-source models do not generalize across the diverse datasets in the benchmark, training on MillionTrees improves both within-domain and out-of-domain performance. Held-out validation datasets using ground truth derived from terrestrial LiDAR paired with overhead RGB show that overfitting to test data is common and hyperparameter tuning is an underappreciated challenge towards a global zero shot tree detection method. We discuss the limitations of the currently available data for airborne RGB tree detection, how to create more robust evaluation data and the need for better understanding of the uncertainty and utility of tree detection from airborne remote sensing.

title: Optimal Conservation Prioritization for Waterfowl and Other Birds in Eastern Canada
content: Conserving and restoring high-quality habitat is widely recognized as one of the most effective means of supporting migratory and wetland bird populations. To advance this objective at a regional scale, the Eastern Habitat Joint Venture (EHJV) coordinates conservation planning for 22 focal bird species across the eastern provinces of Canada. Optimization approaches to support conservation planning are increasingly common, and can be especially valuable in large areas where resources are limited. We present an optimized geospatial prioritization scheme designed to identify regions of primary importance to species coverage objectives within the EHJV. We apply linear programming methods to species abundance data products to maximize population coverage using an adaptable variable-target approach, whose outputs generalize readily to delivery projects of any budget or coverage goal. Our base results highlight areas of high conservation value for priority waterfowl and non-waterfowl species, and we present additional examples of how region-wide solutions can be subdivided based on jurisdictional boundaries, land ownership, or existing protected status. We also address methodological decision points, with attention to how available species abundance data sources were evaluated and what considerations were involved in formulating the optimization computations. We emphasize possibilities for future work to incorporate additional conservation values, such as carbon storage and flood mitigation, and costs, such as land value, and feasibility.

title: Individual-specific recovery of the healthy human gut microbiota after antibiotics
content: Following disruption by broad-spectrum antibiotics, the human gut microbiome undergoes a prolonged recovery where coarse ecological features, such as species richness and diversity, are largely restored. However, as these features are shared by most healthy individuals, it remains unclear whether, even after strong perturbation, individuals preferentially return toward their own pre-treatment composition ('individual-specific recovery') or instead switch to alternative equally healthy states. Resolving this question is fundamental for evaluating the long-term impacts of antibiotics, because an individual's health is affected by their unique microbiome composition, affecting immune regulation and metabolic processing, so a state switch, even to a broadly healthy configuration, could carry unintended consequences. Here we compare each subject's post-antibiotic endpoint with their own baseline and with the baselines of every other subject, across four cohorts (n = 121) whose regimens ranged from a five-day fluoroquinolone course to a four-day three-drug combination given to deplete the gut community. The recovered community was significantly closer to the subject's own baseline than to the alternative healthy baselines in more than 90% of individuals under the mildest regimen and in two thirds of those under regimens that broadly target the gut anaerobes, remaining above chance in every cohort and the majority outcome even where most baseline taxa fell below detection during treatment. This specificity is not merely the persistence and fast regrowth of survivors: it persists among baseline taxa that remain undetected for weeks to months, and the same taxon re-establishes more readily in a host where it was previously detected than in one where it was not. Newly established taxa are consistently more functionally similar to the pre-treatment community than transient arrivals, and their identity correlates with the surviving community's composition in a substantial fraction of subjects. State switching, in contrast, was uncommon and occurred almost exclusively among subjects with the largest reduction in detected taxa during the treatment. Together, these observations reveal the individual-specific nature of the microbiome resilience to broad-spectrum antibiotics, whereas the compositional changes are not random but rather functionally and ecologically associated with the subject's baseline.

title: Enhancing Germination and Assessing the Longevity of Native Plants' Seeds with Dormancy through Different Priming Techniques
content: Vachellia pachyceras and Convolvulus oxyphyllus are native species of arid and semi-arid desert regions, including Kuwait. They are inherently adapted to extreme conditions characterized by high temperature, prolonged drought and limited rainfall. They contribute significantly, to restore the ecosystem by providing food and shelter for wildlife. Despite their ecological importance, seed germination in both species is constrained by dormancy, and natural recruitment of seedlings is limited by narrow and unpredictable rainfall windows, severely restricting opportunities for establishment. In this context, seed priming is an effective pre-sowing technique that enables uniform and rapid germination within the short window of favorable conditions. This study aims to identify the optimal seed-priming techniques for these two keystone native species and to assess the effect of priming on seed longevity. The seeds were scarified to remove the physical dormancy prior to priming treatments. Relative seed longevity was measured for primed seeds through artificial ageing and analyzed using probit analysis and analysis of variance. Results showed that hormonal priming [(mechanical scarification + 100 ppm gibberellic acid (GA3)] for six hours and hydropriming (mechanical scarification + soaking in water) for 8 hours (h) were effective treatments among the tested priming treatments for V. pachyceras. The estimated p50 value (i.e., number of days to lose seed viability to 50%) was 22 days for hormonal priming and 21 days for hydropriming. Mechanical scarification followed by one and half hour of hydropriming was the most effective in C. oxyphyllus (p50 = 74 days). Based on these results, the longevity of V. pachyceras and C. oxyphyllus could be considered  medium. Further studies are needed to determine the effectiveness of seed priming on additional ecologically and economically important native species to achieve success in revegetation programs.

title: Evaluating the Behavior of 230Th and 3He Constant‐Flux Proxies Across a Carbonate Preservation Gradient in the Cocos Ridge
content:
Abstract
We present a comparison of extraterrestrial 3He (3HeET) and excess 230Th (230Thxs) as constant flux proxies across a depth transect on the Cocos Ridge, evaluating their behavior as a function of carbonate dissolution and lateral sediment redistribution. Overall, 60% of paired 3HeET‐ and 230Thxs‐derived mass accumulation rate (MAR) estimates overlap within 1σ uncertainty, indicating broad agreement between the two systems. However, statistically significant discordances between He‐ and Th‐derived MARs occur in three of four cores, with He‐derived MARs exceeding Th‐derived MARs at the ridge crest (positive ΔMAR values) and falling below Th‐derived MARs at flank sites (negative ΔMAR). The discordance at the ridge crest is consistent with sediment winnowing and preferential removal of 3He‐bearing particles, whereas the smaller discordances in flank cores are best explained by a complementary focusing signal, likely reflecting redistribution of material removed from the ridge top. Evaluation of the negative ΔMAR offsets demonstrates that 230Thxs is effectively retained during carbonate dissolution, as ΔMAR responses remain small despite strong CaCO3 preservation gradients, and theoretical constraints indicate negligible thorium mobility. When applied jointly, the two proxies provide complementary constraints on MARs that would remain unresolved using a single proxy. However, their interpretation remains site‐dependent, requiring careful consideration of sediment composition, transport regime, and analytical limitations. Because sedimentary burial fluxes are calculated from component concentrations and MAR, these proxy‐dependent differences directly affect estimates of carbonate and other elemental burial fluxes, with implications for reconstructing both past and modern marine biogeochemical cycles.

title: The Association of Diet, Intestinal Microbial Starch Utilizers and Butyrate‐Producers in Early Life
content:
In vitro, resistant starch cross‐feeding of A. hallii with R. bromii yielded higher amounts of butyrate than with B. adolescentis. At the same time, infants that harboured both starch utilizer and A. hallii had higher faecal butyrate levels than those without these species. Differences in the mode of degradation might support functional redundancy and butyrate formation in early life.

ABSTRACT
During the first year of life, infant diet changes from liquid to solid food. Resistant starch is one of the first complex carbohydrates available to gut microbiota. With the overall goal to gain mechanistic understanding on the development of microbial starch utilization capacity and its impact on fermentation activity, we investigated the interplay of diet, starch utilizers Ruminococcus bromii and Bifidobacterium adolescentis and the butyrate producer Anaerobutyricum hallii using samples from the longitudinal CARE cohort, and in vitro. Infants started to consume resistant starch at 4 months. While less than one quarter of the infants harboured starch utilizers at 5 months, occurrence increased until the end of year one. In vitro, R. bromii and B. adolescentis degraded resistant starch but only R. bromii released reducing sugars. B. adolescentis formed acetate and lactate. In co‐cultures, R. bromii with A. hallii produced more butyrate via reducing sugars than with lactate and acetate from B. adolescentis. At one year of age, infants that harboured both starch utilizer and A. hallii had higher faecal butyrate levels than those without these species. Our results suggest that differences in the mode of resistant starch degradation and cross‐feeding contributed to functional redundancy and affected butyrate formation.

title: Targeted Mutagenesis Reveals Noncanonical Genetic Requirements for Carbon Monoxide Oxidation
content:
Using targeted mutagenesis, this study shows that form II CODH does not contribute to CO oxidation in the model carboxydovore Paraburkholderia terrae COX and reveals that canonical maturation pathways are not universally conserved. These findings refine genome‐based predictions of microbial metabolism and improve understanding of metalloenzyme assembly diversity and evolution.

ABSTRACT
Carbon monoxide (CO) oxidation is a widespread microbial energy metabolism catalysed by MoCu CO dehydrogenase (CODH). Of the two phylogenetically distinct forms (form‐I and form‐II), only form‐I CODH is functionally verified. CODH activity requires maturation of the [CuSMoO2] active site, linked in the carboxydotroph Afipia carboxidovorans OM5 to the genes coxDEF. CODH maturation remains untested outside of this system. Paraburkholderia terrae COX, a recently isolated carboxydovore, encodes both forms of CODH with a reduced and reorganised cox gene cluster. Using targeted mutagenesis, we identify rcoM, coxL, coxF, and coxG as essential for CO oxidation, whereas coxD, coxE, and mocA are non‐essential. Deletion of the accessory coxDEF genes produced distinct phenotypes compared to A. carboxidovorans OM5, revealing alternative routes for CODH maturation. Both coxL paralogs were deleted singly and in double knockouts, providing the first molecular evidence that form‐II CODH does not contribute to CO oxidation in vivo in these groups of bacteria. Together, these findings show that CODH maturation and function are not universally conserved and caution against inferring CO‐oxidising capacity solely from gene presence. Pb. terrae COX emerges as a genetically tractable model for elucidating the diversity and evolution of metalloenzyme assembly pathways in bacteria.

title: Microbial Syntrophy Drives Methanogenesis From Residual Hydrocarbons in Anaerobic Oil Sands Tailings
content:
Methane production from residual hydrocarbons in anaerobic oil sands tailings is shaped by interactions between bacterial and archaeal groups. Shapley‐based attribution reveals differences between microbial contributions and relative abundance, while variation across sites and stages highlights the role of environmental context in methane production and late‐stage prediction.

ABSTRACT
Anaerobic oil sands tailings can generate methane for decades as residual naphtha‐range and petroleum hydrocarbons sustain microbial metabolism, but how microbial interactions link hydrocarbon turnover to methanogenesis remains poorly resolved. To characterize these microbial associations, we analyse two naphtha‐amended anaerobic tailings incubation series using 16S rRNA gene relative abundance, hydrocarbon consumption, and methane production data within a cooperative game‐theoretical framework. The abundance‐informed Shapley analysis attributes system‐level variation to bacterial–archaeal coalitions, highlighting key syntrophic partnerships. Several taxa show inferred contributions to methanogenesis that are disproportionate to their relative abundance, indicating that model‐based attribution can differ from abundance ranking. Sensitivity analysis shows that the main methane‐attribution patterns remain interpretable across alternative abundance‐weighted coefficient formulations. These interaction patterns shift across incubation phases, showing that microbial control over hydrocarbon‐dependent methanogenesis changes through time. When incorporated into stochastic forecasting, Shapley‐derived reaction intensities improve predictive performance compared with reduced microbial and non‐microbial benchmarks. Together, our results indicate that methane production in oil sands tailings can be interpreted through abundance‐informed bacterial–archaeal coalition structure, providing a coalition‐aware basis for interpreting and forecasting methanogenic hydrocarbon transformation.

title: Host Development and Environment Influence the Microbiomes of Aquatic Insects and Riparian Spiders
content:
Aquatic insect larvae had higher microbiome diversity than adult life stages, and there was greater retention of larvae‐derived bacterial taxa in adults of hemi‐ compared to holometabolous insects. Wastewater treatment plant effluents decreased endosymbionts in aquatic insects and increased predicted xenobiotic degradation pathways across larvae, adults, and their terrestrial predators, riparian spiders.

ABSTRACT
Larval aquatic insects harbour diverse microbiomes critical for physiology and development, yet the effects of metamorphosis combined with environmental exposures on this community remain unknown. Herein we examined bacterial microbiome composition and predicted function across larval and adult stages of three families of aquatic insects and riparian spider predators, collected upstream and downstream of wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) in Ontario, Canada. Insect host developmental stage was the primary driver of microbiome structure. Larval microbiomes were more diverse and showed higher abundances in pathways reflecting active feeding. Larval and adult populations of holometabolous insects shared few ASVs (3.8%–12.6% of the combined ASV pool), whereas a larger proportion was shared in hemimetabolous insects (23.4%). WWTP effluent exposures led to selective microbial filtering rather than broad community restructuring. Macroinvertebrate and spider microbiomes sampled downstream were characterized by higher abundances in bacterial taxa associated with wastewaters and increased xenobiotic degradation pathways. Such impacts on spider microbiomes provide evidence that ecological impacts of effluents cross the aquatic‐terrestrial boundary. Lastly, a significant decrease of vertically transmitted endosymbionts (Rickettsiella, Wolbachia) was detected in aquatic insects, representing a pathway through which effluent pollution may affect host fitness without detectably altering overall microbiome diversity.

title: The Broad Ecological Range of Salmonella enterica Serotype Typhimurium Is Associated With Genomic Diversification
content:
The broad ecological range of Salmonella enterica serotype Typhimurium is associated with dynamic gain and loss of accessory genes, including plasmid‐associated antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, along with positive selection on core genes, potentially contributing to its differential adaptation across food animal and non‐food animal reservoirs. This genomic diversification allows for the identification of genetic variants predictive of isolation source using machine learning models. Created in BioRender. Liao (2026) https://BioRender.com/oroohp1.

ABSTRACT
Salmonella Typhimurium is a versatile foodborne pathogen with a broad ecological range, making it an ideal model to better understand pathogen adaptations that allow them to infect multiple hosts and persist across environments. Here, we analysed 595 genomes of S. Typhimurium representing three food animal sources (bovine, swine, and poultry) and one non‐food animal source (wild birds). We found that S. Typhimurium from food animal sources generally had a more open pangenome and harboured more antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). Notably, swine isolates exhibited the most open pangenome and the highest prevalence of ARGs, patterns that were associated with a greater presence of mobile genetic elements, particularly plasmids. Despite similar core genome sizes, S. Typhimurium from different sources displayed distinct patterns of positive selection in the core genome that varied in frequency and targeted functional categories. In contrast, although accessory genome sizes varied substantially across sources, the frequency of positive selection remained similar. Using machine learning, we identified source‐predictive genetic variants, many of which are associated with stress‐response functions. These findings suggest that gain and loss of accessory genes and positive selection acting on core genes support differential adaptation in S. Typhimurium, potentially contributing to its broad ecological range.

title: Functional Genomics of a Zinc‐Solubilising Kosakonia cowanii RL‐16 and Its Application for Zinc Biofortification in Oryza sativa L.
content:
Genome analysis of Kosakonia cowanii RL‐16 revealed mechanisms associated with zinc solubilisation. RL‐16 enhanced zinc bioavailability in rhizospheric soil, demonstrating its potential to improve zinc biofortification in rice (Oryza sativa L.). These findings highlight RL‐16 as a promising microbial candidate for rice grain zinc enrichment.

ABSTRACT
Zinc (Zn) is assumed to be the most important micronutrient due to its involvement in different biochemical processes. The daily requirement of Zn for the human body, however, cannot be fulfilled by traditional staple crops such as rice due to its low availability to plants, especially in alkaline soils. The present study was carried out to investigate the potential of indigenous microbial flora, isolated from different agroecological zones, for Zn solubilization and combating Zn deficiency in rice. Out of a total of 135 isolates, RL‐16, identified as Kosakonia cowanii, emerged as the most valuable resource for sustainable agricultural applications due to its incredible Zn solubilization potential and additional PGP characteristics. Gene mining of RL‐16 revealed the footprints of solubilization of Zn and other nutrients. Under microcosmic conditions, zinc content was significantly improved for the treatment with RL‐16 (134.7 mg/kg ± 0.6), compared to the control containing only an insoluble zinc source (107.7 mg/kg ± 1.6). Zinc translocation in seed (ZnSd) was enhanced by the application of RL‐16 across both varieties, which was also confirmed by field evaluation. This study demonstrates the whole genome sequence analysis of Kosakonia cowanii and its potential role in Zn biofortification for more targeted and sustainable agricultural practices.

title: Seasonal and Environmental Influences on Microbial Community Dynamics in the Dunk River Watershed, Prince Edward Island, Canada
content:
We characterized the taxonomic diversity of river microbial communities across diverse sites using high‐throughput sequencing. Our findings demonstrate that environmental drivers—from seasonal cycles to farm‐level inputs—predictably reshape the bacterial landscape, providing a framework for monitoring aquatic ecosystem dynamics.

ABSTRACT
Riverine ecosystems are crucial biogeochemical hubs, with their microbial communities playing a key role in nutrient cycling and overall ecosystem health. This study used shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize the seasonal and environmental drivers of taxonomic and functional microbial community structure (read depth between 1.91 and 30.44 bp) in four tributaries of the Dunk River watershed in Prince Edward Island (PEI), a landscape shaped by intensive agriculture and groundwater‐dominated streamflow, where the seasonal and land‐use impacts on the river's microbiome remain understudied. Although taxonomic composition showed no significant spatial variation among sampling sites, functional profiling identified subtle but distinct spatial signatures, primarily driven at the site with the least human impacts. Mass effects driven by above‐ or below‐ground water dispersal pathways may override local selective pressures, resulting in a more uniform community structure across different locations. The study also identified significant correlations between certain rare microbial taxa and nutrient concentrations. This work provides critical baseline data on microbial ecology in PEI river systems, indicating that while temporal factors are the primary identifiable drivers among the measured variables, a substantial majority of the community variance remains unexplained, likely reflecting the inherent stochasticity of open riverine ecosystems.

title: Issue Information
Phenology and surface energy balance changes across northern lands
content:
Phenology and surface energy balance changes across northern lands
Olivia Hau, Matthias Forkel, Wolfgang Buermann, Johanna Kranz, Mirco Migliavacca, Ulrich Weber, Annu Panwar, and Alexander Josef Winkler
Biogeosciences, 23, 7705–7725, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7705-2026, 2026
Shifts in spring and autumn growth due to climate warming change how plants reflect sunlight and release heat and moisture into the air, modulating surface warming. The strength of these effects and their regional variability remain poorly understood. Using satellite and climate data, we show that earlier spring growth increases moisture release, especially in forests, while autumn changes are smaller and less consistent. Impacts on land-atmosphere interactions vary by ecosystem and data source.

title: Expansion of the Wave Action Season Across Alaska's Marginal Seas
content:
Abstract
Rapid loss of Arctic sea ice is transforming wave dynamics across Alaska's marginal seas, expanding the period when surface waves actively develop and propagate. This study quantifies how the wave action season (WAS) has evolved in the past 45 years across northern and western Alaska using a multi‐decadal hindcast validated against satellite altimetry from the ESA Climate Change Initiative and ICESat‐2 ATL12 data sets. Utilizing the coupled ADCIRC‐SWAN model, it accurately reproduces the spatial distribution and magnitude of observed wave heights, providing a basis for assessing temporal and spatial trends in the WAS characteristics. Results show a consistent regional expansion of the WAS throughout Alaska. The onset of wave activity has advanced by approximately 0.8–2.0 days·yr−1 across the Chukchi and Beaufort Seas, with localized maxima near Wainwright exceeding 2 days·yr−1. The end of the season has been delayed by up to 1.4 days·yr−1, yielding a net lengthening of 1–2 days·yr−1 across most of the state's nearshore areas. These changes result in total lengthening exceeding 100 days in parts of the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas over the past 45 years. Duration trends form a continuous corridor of positive change along the Chukchi and Beaufort Seas and gradually weaken southward into the northern Bering Sea. These results demonstrate that the WAS has expanded consistently across Alaska's marginal seas over the last four decades, reflecting a sustained shift toward longer periods of active wave development as sea‐ice retreat extends fetch.

title: Folding without glutamine: Proteome-scale removal of a canonical amino acid
content:
by Alejandro Garciarrubio, Blanca Ramos-Cerrillo, Enrique Morett, Lorenzo Segovia

All known life uses a canonical alphabet of 20 amino acids, yet which residues are structurally essential remains untested at proteome scale. Isoleucine was recently eliminated from ribosomal proteins in Escherichia coli, establishing that amino acid alphabet reduction is feasible. Here we ask whether an entire amino acid can be eliminated from a proteome, and develop a computational framework to identify the best target. Using two independent approaches — ProteinMPNN structure-based probabilities and multiple sequence alignment conservation — we define “keep-score” as the fraction of positions where the native residue is optimal. Both methods converge on an unexpected candidate: glutamine has the lowest keep-score, with proline and glycine the highest — counter to substitution-matrix intuition. Glutamine’s low keep-score is not explained by a single obvious substitute; glutamate is preferred in only 14% of replacements. Removing this target proteome-wide, we replaced every glutamine across 4,148 proteins with ProteinMPNN-optimal alternatives and modeled the resulting sequences with AlphaFold2. The recoded proteome maintained native-like structures: 85.5% of models exceeded a TMscore of 0.8, indistinguishable from the 85.9% baseline for rebuilt native sequences. Orthogonal validation — ESMFold predictions, Rosetta energy calculations, and conformational ensemble comparisons — revealed no evidence of systematic misfolding attributable to glutamine removal. As a consistency check, a glutamine-free TEM-1 β-lactamase designed with ProteinMPNN conferred ampicillin resistance in E. coli, indicating fold preservation can extend to biological function. Evolutionary evidence further supports these findings: 24% of E. coli proteins have glutamine-free orthologs in prokaryotic genomes, and glutamine ranks lowest in keep-score in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. These results show that an entire amino acid can be removed from a proteome with folds broadly preserved, establishing keep-score as a general framework and glutamine as the primary candidate for recoding. Crucially, this reflects a computational analysis of structural replaceability, not a demonstration of biological dispensability.

title: The influence of ensemble size and composition on the performance of combined real-time COVID-19 forecasts
content:
by Friederike Becker, Katharine Sherratt, Nikos I. Bosse, Sebastian Funk

During infectious disease outbreaks, short-term forecasts can play an important role for both decision makers and the general public. While previous research has shown that combining individual forecasts into an ensemble improves accuracy and consistency, practical guidance for organisers of multi-model prediction platforms on how to construct an ensemble has been scarce. In particular, it is not entirely clear how ensemble performance relates to the size of the underlying model pool, a relevant question when relying on voluntary contributions from modelling teams that face competing priorities. Furthermore, the exact composition of an ensemble forecast may influence its performance. Ensembles can either include all models equally or, alternatively, discriminate based on past performance or other characteristics. Using data from the European COVID-19 Forecast Hub we investigated these questions, with the aim of offering practical guidance to organisers of multi-model prediction platforms during infectious disease outbreaks. We found that including more models both improved and stabilised aggregate ensemble performance, while selecting for better component models did not yield any particular advantage. Diversity among models, whether measured numerically or qualitatively, did not have a clear impact on ensemble performance. These results suggest that for those soliciting contributions to collaborative ensembles there are more obvious gains to be made from increasing participation to moderate levels than from optimising component models.

title: Global sensitivity analysis for stochastic models of infectious diseases: Re-emergence of yellow fever virus in the Americas as a case study
content:
by Nate Kornetzke, Helen J. Wearing

Emerging infectious diseases are a persistent public health threat that challenge deterministic, mechanistic modeling approaches. Because outbreaks initially start with a low number of infected hosts, their dynamics are highly stochastic, making traditional deterministic methods, e.g., ordinary differential equations, unable to qualitatively or quantitatively capture the transmission dynamics. In place, stochastic models are used, such as Markov chain models, but these models present their own challenges. Often, to infer a quantity of interest with stochastic models, we need to sample the model’s distribution many times over, introducing an additional source of noise to our analysis. This additional noise makes the inference of our quantity of interest more difficult and computationally expensive. Here, we show how novel tools from the field of uncertainty quantification can be used to efficiently separate these two channels of noise, allowing us to make rigorous statistical inferences about processes important for disease emergence. We illustrate these techniques with a model of yellow fever virus spillover in the Americas, a virus that has seen rapid re-emergence amongst multiple hosts and vectors in South America over the last decade. We show that only a handful of parameters’ uncertainties greatly affect variation in cumulative disease incidence. In particular, uncertainty in patch connectivity and non-human primate latency has the greatest impact on the variation of cumulative disease incidence of yellow fever virus across patches.

title: A split nozzle and two-protein chain-like fibers define the tail architecture of Pseudomonas aeruginosa podophage A1002
content:
by Hao Pang, Yuan Chen, Zeng Peng, Hao Xiao, Wenyuan Chen, Xiaowu Li, Ping Chen, Jing Zheng, Hongrong Liu

Phage therapy offers unique advantages against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, high-resolution structural studies of phages targeting Pseudomonas aeruginosa—a top-seven global pathogen—particularly podophages, remain severely limited, directly impeding structure-based development of novel antimicrobials. In this study, we utilize cryo-EM to resolve the high-resolution intact structure of mature phage A1002, a podophage infecting carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa. Based on density maps combined with AlphaFold3 predictions, we identified 11 structural protein components from the head to the tail. Phage A1002 exhibits a distinctly elongated tail morphology distinct from other reported podophages. Notably, the A1002 nozzle employs a distinct assembly strategy, featuring the unique nozzle-rope protein and nozzle-base protein, which may have evolved through modular evolution and horizontal gene transfer. Furthermore, the nozzle-rope protein provides 11 adsorption sites for fiber dimers, and these dimers are assembled from two proteins, giving rise to two types of dimers: dimers 1–7 correspond to fiber I (gp40), and dimers 8–11 correspond to fiber II (gp41). The nozzle-rope protein and these dimers combine to form a chain-like fiber. The tail tube comprises a double-layered, elongated tube structure that functions to simultaneously increase tail length and provide docking sites for six chain-like fibers. These distinctive structural features provide the molecular basis for A1002’s broad-spectrum infection of drug-resistant P. aeruginosa and offer a novel molecular blueprint for rational design of structure-guided phage therapeutics.

title: An open-source eye-tracking system adaptable to diverse terrestrial vertebrates reveals state-dependent visual acquisition in lizards
content:
by Nimrod Leberstein, Tali Remenick, Milan Becker, Mark Shein-Idelson

Gaze shifts are fundamental to visual exploration and processing, yet empirical knowledge is largely confined to a small number of model species, limiting our understanding of general principles of visual acquisition across animals. Here, we introduce a versatile, low-cost, and open-source framework design for eye-tracking in small, freely moving animals. Leveraging photogrammetry, 3D modeling, and 3D-printing, we produce headmounts adaptable to diverse head-eye geometries, as we demonstrate for lizards, turtles, and mice. Detailed recordings in Pogona vitticeps, a laterally eyed ectotherm with a high-acuity retina, reveal a rich oculomotor repertoire with kinematics closely resembling the saccadic main sequence in primates. We found both movement-coupled large binocular saccades, which exhibited a strong axial bias as well as small, isotropic, and monocular saccades suggesting a capacity for visual exploration of local details. Visual acquisition strategies were strongly tied to behavioral states with periods of active sampling (3–5 Hz saccades) separated by periods of ocular stillness lasting many seconds and suggesting a visual acquisition strategy distinct from those commonly described in endothermic model species. Furthermore, active states were correlated with pupil constriction in contrast to mammals and similarly to birds. Our results demonstrate the utility of our experimental approach for understanding visual acquisition across terrestrial vertebrates. Such a multi-perspective view on natural visual acquisition across species will be essential for developing a generalized understanding of vision, its ecological functions, and its evolutionary trajectory.

title: The human hippocampus supports auditory coding and multisensory integration
content:
by Omri Raccah, Aryan Agarwal, Yannan Zhu, Nicholas B. Turk-Browne

The hippocampus receives convergent input from multiple sensory systems, yet in humans it has been studied almost exclusively through vision. Here we examine how the hippocampus contributes to sensory processing beyond the visual modality and to the multisensory integration of visual information with these other modalities. Participants were exposed to multiple repetitions of short naturalistic movie clips, each presented in four formats: auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, and incongruent audiovisual (audio and video from different movies). Using high-resolution fMRI, we measured univariate activation and multivariate representations across the longitudinal axis and subfields of the human hippocampus. Whereas univariate analyses detected only visual responses across hippocampal subregions, with no activation for auditory stimuli and no benefit of congruent stimuli, multivariate analyses revealed robust representations of both auditory and visual scenes. The posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli relative to unisensory stimuli, especially in the left hemisphere, demonstrating multisensory facilitation. The anterior hippocampus showed crossmodal decoding between auditory and visual versions of the same clip, driven by the right hemisphere, suggesting a more abstract representation. Finally, whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed parallel effects in cortical regions known to support multisensory integration. These findings advance understanding of auditory and multisensory coding in the human hippocampus, revealing specialization and lateralization along its longitudinal axis.

title: A deep genetic structure phylogenomically frames the closest algal relatives of land plants
content:
by Maaike J. Bierenbroodspot, Cäcilia F. Kunz, Elisa S. Goldbecker, Maike Lorenz, Iker Irisarri, Thomas Pröschold, Tatyana Darienko, Jan de Vries

Discerning the nature of the last common ancestor of land plants (embryophytes) and algae allows to retrace the adaptations that ushered in the conquest of land by plants. For this, the closest streptophyte algal relatives of embryophytes hold key information. Albeit initially coming as a surprise due to their plain body plans, all major phylogenomic efforts have concluded that the Zygnematophyceae are the algal sisters to land plants. The Zygnematophyceae are the streptophyte algal class with the greatest species richness and while we now have ample genome information on a few select members of zygnematophytes, our understanding of the genomic divergence as well as genetic potential for key traits is limited by a lack of phylodiverse data that accounts for this diversity and integrates it into a phylogenomic framework. We here sequenced 43 new transcriptome datasets for the Zygnematophyceae and built a phylogenomic tree based on a total of 104 zygnematophyceaen transcriptomes and 2243 loci. We recover a deep genetic structure for the Zygnematophyceae: Despite the deep split between Spirogyrales and their unicellular sister group Desmidiales, most Spirogyrales emerged after pronounced genetic divergence, accommodating the attainment of multicellularity and divergent traits such as unique cell and plastid division. Overall, our data capture signatures of massive ancient radiations that could only be revealed thanks to a phylodiverse sampling. Recognizing the deep genetic divergences and a vast evolutionary history of the Zygnematophyceae are key to illuminate the nature of the algal progenitors of land plants.

title: Infant presence and mother-infant conflict predict fetal loss in wild mandrills
content:
by Nikolaos Smit, Berta Roura-Torres, Axelle Delaunay, Alice Baniel, Elise Huchard, Marie J. E. Charpentier

Female fitness depends on reproductive pace and offspring survival, both of which are determined by the ability to balance resource allocation between current and future reproduction. Using 11 years of data on 356 pregnancies (52 of which resulted in fetal loss) from 117 wild female mandrills, we show that females who conceive while still caring for a young infant experience a greater probability of fetal loss as well as increased mother-infant behavioral conflict in the form of maternal rejection. In addition, females whose infants throw more tantrums show a greater probability of fetal loss, consistent with observations from other species where living offspring can interfere in parental reproduction. Finally, females who lose a fetus show greater subsequent reproductive success (produce more surviving infants and show shorter inter-birth intervals) than females who give birth but their infants die soon after birth. These findings suggest that fetal loss may represent an adaptive physiological response to the energetic constraints imposed by overlapping gestation and maternal care, potentially limiting the fitness costs associated with short inter-birth intervals and concurrent investment in multiple dependent offspring.

title: Spyglass is a framework for reproducible and shareable neuroscience research
content: Scientific progress depends on reliable and reproducible results. Progress can be accelerated when data are shared and re-analyzed to address new questions. Current approaches to storing and analyzing neural data involve bespoke formats and software that make replication and reuse of data difficult. To address these challenges, we created Spyglass, an open-source data management and analysis framework written in Python. Spyglass provides reproducible pipelines for common neuroscience analyses and sharing of raw data, intermediate analyses, and final results within and across labs. Spyglass uses the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) standard and includes pipelines for spectral filtering, spike sorting, pose tracking, and neural decoding. Spyglass can be extended to apply existing and newly developed pipelines to datasets from multiple sources. We demonstrate these features in the context of a cross-laboratory replication by applying advanced state space decoding algorithms to publicly available data. New users can try out Spyglass on a Jupyter Hub hosted by HHMI and 2i2c: https://spyglass.hhmi.2i2c.cloud/.

title: A validated antibody toolbox for ALS research
content: A substantial fraction of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated proteins remains poorly characterized, in part because of the limited availability of validated research antibodies. We established knockout (KO)-based antibody characterization workflows and demonstrated that widely used antibodies against the major ALS-associated protein C9orf72 lacked specificity (Laflamme et al., 2019). We subsequently scaled this framework to systematically benchmark research antibodies, revealing that up to 61% fail to perform as recommended by manufacturers (Ayoubi et al., 2023b). Here, we extend this approach by establishing the ALS-Reproducible Antibody Platform (ALS-RAP), a comprehensive effort to generate a publicly available dataset of KO-validated antibodies targeting proteins encoded by ALS risk genes. In total, we characterized 303 antibodies against 33 ALS-associated proteins to identify high-quality reagents for use in western blot, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence. Using these antibodies, we profiled protein levels across human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary neurological cell types. These analyses revealed diverse cellular distributions and higher levels of several ALS-associated proteins in glial populations, consistent with emerging evidence for immune contributions to ALS. Together, ALS-RAP provides a validated antibody toolbox and protein expression resource to support the study of ALS-associated proteins.

title: Prevalence of Local Emissions in Arctic Carbonaceous Aerosols Revealed by Dual Carbon Isotopes and Atmospheric Transport Modeling
content:
Abstract
Carbonaceous aerosols in the Arctic are mainly attributed to long‐range transport from lower latitudes, but direct observational data over the central Arctic Ocean, particularly in summer, remain limited. We present a cruise‐based study conducted during the eighth Xuelong Arctic expedition across the central Arctic Ocean. Using dual carbon isotope analysis (δ13C– Δ14C), molecular organic composition, and black carbon (BC)‐atmospheric modeling, we provide quantitative insights into the sources of Arctic marine aerosols. Our findings show significant spatial differences in aerosol composition between the North Pacific and Arctic Ocean. Fossil fuel–derived carbon contributes 55.5 ± 17% (0.49 ± 0.39 μg m−3) of total carbon in Arctic summer aerosols. While model simulations closely match BC concentrations outside the Arctic Ocean, they underestimate BC levels in the inner Arctic by a factor of two, suggesting gaps in local source representation. These findings emphasize the need for better representation of local emissions, especially from shipping, in models to improve understanding of aerosol‐driven climate effects in the Arctic.

title: Impact of Reservoirs on Streamflow Extremes in India
content:
Abstract
India has an extensive network of reservoirs, yet their influence on streamflow extremes remains poorly quantified. To understand how reservoirs have altered the natural flow regime across India, we integrate 223 reservoirs into a national hydrologic modeling system integrating Noah‐MP land surface model and MizuRoute hydrodynamic model. Including reservoirs improved national streamflow NSE by 43%. The results reveal that reservoirs provide 46.1% median attenuation of monsoon high flow peaks and a 235% augmentation of pre‐monsoon low flows. Large reservoirs (≥1000 MCM) dominate magnitude control of extremes while smaller reservoirs (<1000 MCM) drive the 1–3 days onset lag. Alarmingly, 74% of reservoirs reach near full capacity next day immediately after a high flow peak. This systematic saturation leaves the network highly vulnerable to sequential high inflows, necessitating a shift toward forecast‐informed operations to mitigate risk.

title: Sparse‐Well Diffusion Reconstructions Enable Groundwater Transport Equation Recovery and Plume Refinement
content:
Abstract
Groundwater contamination assessments based on sparse wells rarely provide continuous hydraulic head and contaminant concentration fields for plume interpretation. Visually plausible reconstructions may not retain the transport information needed for physical diagnosis. We develop a Sparse‐Well Diffusion‐SINDy Residual Refinement (SW‐DSRR) framework that couples diffusion reconstruction, Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics transport equation recovery and consistency assessment, and consistency‐guided plume refinement to test whether sparse‐well reconstructions preserve transport structure. This information is then used to reduce plume error. Tests cover normal and extreme well layouts under baseline, source/sink, and heterogeneous permeability conditions. Reconstructed fields retain dominant terms, generating parameter scales, and hidden contaminant source structure. Recovered equations reproduce observed‐well and full‐field evolution while preserving mass, centroid migration, and nonnegative concentrations. Relative to initial diffusion reconstructions, plume refinement reduces concentration errors. SW‐DSRR connects field reconstruction with equation‐level assessment and targeted plume correction that can support plume delineation, source assessment, and remediation planning.

content:

Juan Usó-Canós, Enrique Isla, Isabelle Peeters, and Karima López
