title: Stochastic and Heritable Responses in Cell-Size Regulation and Survival to pH Stress in C. glutamicum
content: Bacterial survival in fluctuating environments depends on the ability of individual cells to maintain physiological homeostasis under stress, yet how single cells recover from transient pH fluctuations remains poorly understood. We tracked the cell-size dynamics and survival of Corynebacterium glutamicum cells exposed to short, strong acid (pH 4, 20 min) or alkaline (pH 11, 15 min) pulses. Acid stress considerably increases the size added during the stress cycle, whereas alkaline stress increases it only modestly. Nevertheless, surviving cells maintain their division strategy and restore size homeostasis in the next cycle. Coordination between relatives is short-lived: sister cells have similar cell-cycle durations after stress, but durations become uncorrelated once the last division shared by two cells precedes the stress by more than about 1.5 generations. Survival of acid stress favors larger cells and is largely stochastic, with no detectable lineage heritability. In contrast, survival of alkaline stress favors smaller cells and is transiently heritable: co-survival probability remains high among relatives separated by up to two generations. These findings provide insight into pH survival in C. glutamicum and present statistical methods to study cell-size regulation and survival under transient, severe environmental fluctuations.

title: A Systems Theory of Cardiac-Autonomic Trajectories and Equilibria
content: Heart rate variability (HRV) is conventionally summarized with static indices computed over fixed windows, which cannot show how cardiac autonomic regulation persists, transitions, responds to perturbation, and recovers. We develop the Systems Theory of Cardiac-Autonomic Trajectories and Equilibria (STATE), in which autonomic regulation is a low-dimensional latent stochastic dynamical system observed only through RR intervals, and we derive what the theory can and cannot claim. First, we prove that for isotropic linear dynamics the sympathetic and parasympathetic coordinates are not separately identifiable from a scalar RR signal, whereas distinct time scales or coupling restore observability. Second, we derive exact properties of a minimal bistable system (stationary law, mean escape time, critical forcing), and a Monte Carlo simulation agreed with the exact escape time within 6%. Third, in 2000 simulated replicates of a monostable and a bistable system that share the same linearization at rest, baseline variability (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC, 0.56) and peak displacement at the pulse used (AUC 0.42) did not discriminate the systems, yet sustained return after an identical pulse differed: 100% versus 7%. We define resilience as a multidimensional response profile, show that recovery descriptors depend on analyst-chosen tolerances that must be fixed a priori, and state four falsifiable hypotheses with the result that would refute each. The work is theoretical and computational; no empirical recordings were used.

title: Emergence and robustness of 3D complex tissue architectures from simple physical forces
content: Although at central stake in biology and biological engineering, our understanding of how biological tissues acquire their architectures during morphogenesis and which mechanisms have been selected through evolution remain limited. Using adipose tissue as a biological model, we build a 3D mathematical model with simple mechanical rules between cells and fibers, and show that the model reproduces, in-silico, not only the emergence of complex and heterogeneous 3D architectures, but also the intra and inter-individual heterogeneities of shapes as observed in vivo. The model reveals that specific rules for cell differentiation are not necessary for tissue structuring, but could have been selected through evolution for robustness and efficiency. This study therefore suggests a paradigm shift where tissue architecture is an emerging process surprisingly more driven by mechanical processes than by complex predetermined molecular or genetic programs.

title: Organelle Aging Predicts Human Disease
content: Aging affects cellular organelles differently, but whether subcellular aging predicts human disease remains unknown. Here, we integrated organelle-enriched proteins in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid proteomes from 61,931 individuals to model aging of 10 organelles across the human lifespan. Organelle aging was heterogeneous with lysosomes, plasma membranes, and Golgi compartments accelerating rapidly after age 60. Individuals with four or more prematurely aged compartments exhibited up to 22-fold higher kidney disease risk and up to 8-fold higher mortality risk. Major diseases are characterized by distinct organelle aging signatures and disease risk increased with the number of accelerated organelles. APOE-{varepsilon}4 dosage was associated with lysosomal and mitochondrial aging and reduced PDP1 levels, implicating altered energy metabolism. Decomposition of organelle signature coefficients into biological programs further showed that diseases are associated with distinct subcellular patterns. These findings establish organelle-resolved aging as a measurable dimension of human biology, revealing subcellular mechanisms underlying disease susceptibility and resilience.

title: Simulating the dynamics of gene regulatory systems at cellular scale
content: The temporal nature of eukaryotic gene expression is the result of a complex, non-linear, dynamical system of regulatory processes. So far, models of such systems trade realism for tractability by using strict simplifying assumptions. These simplified models are often unfaithful to our biological understanding; however, without such simplifications, analytical solutions become more challenging and these dynamical systems must then be studied through simulation. Here, we explore the question of how this complex web of gene regulatory connections can be faithfully simulated for all tens of thousands of genes that usually define a eukaryotic organism. We present a proof-of-principle model and simulator, GeneRegulatorySystems.jl which is based on a biophysical chemical master equation that overcomes three key restrictions. First, it allows an exact stochastic simulation of fully non-linear gene expression dynamics, including feedback control, to parsimoniously capture cause and effect relationships of gene regulation. Further, it includes a general framework for implementing diverse mechanisms of gene control such as protein mediated degradation, RNAi, and protein complex formation. Finally, it scales realistically to tens of thousands of genes. We achieve this by introducing a domain-specific programming language to aid the design of experimental protocols from small-scale, well-studied, scenarios of gene regulation inspired by dynamical systems biology up to large-scale, single cell omics experiments with interventions. In this way, our framework provides a grammar of in silico experimental design that can capture single-cell gene expression dynamics for entire genomes.

title: Mixing, competence, and commitment set the stability of cell identity
content: Cells maintain their identities in the face of molecular noise, yet can change them rapidly when cued. Here, we treat this tension as a problem in the control of a stochastic system. We represent a cell identity as a set of molecular configurations, or microstates, among which cells undergo stochastic transitions, and measure its stability by the effective rate of commitment to another identity, using a Markov model in which committed cells are removed. Mixing, competence, and commitment provide three channels for tuning this rate. They govern microstate transitions, how commitment is distributed among microstates, and the overall speed of commitment, respectively. Control over the effective commitment rate is shared between commitment and mixing in proportions that always sum to one. Interventions with the same effective commitment rate cannot be told apart by survival alone but, given the microstate transition rates, can be distinguished by the fraction of cells in each microstate or by how quickly cells sorted on permissive microstates commit. When competence varies in time, pulsed commitment signalling commits more cells than sustained signalling of equal dose, by an amount that grows with the depth of that variation, whereas with constant competence pulsing gains nothing in the models we studied. This suggests a possible function for pulsatile signalling, such as that of ERK, which the experiments we propose could test. Finally, reanalysing single-cell imaging of mouse embryonic stem cells leaving naive pluripotency, we estimate that cells take about as long to acquire competence as they then wait to commit, and we specify experiments to identify which channel drives this exit.

title: Enzyme-Constrained Metabolic Modeling Reveals CO2-Dependent Growth Control in Picochlorum celeri
content: Picochlorum celeri grows 11.6 times faster at elevated CO2 than in air, yet the abundance of its metabolic enzymes is only 17% higher. To explain this, we reconstructed iPiccel954, a genome-scale metabolic model with 3525 reactions, 2973 metabolites and 954 genes, and eciPiccel954, its enzyme-constrained version limited by the measured enzyme abundance in air and at elevated CO2. Calibrating the enzyme-constrained models against the measured proteome showed that a similar protein budget supports very different growth depending on how it is allocated. With urea as the nitrogen source, urea carboxylase was the only step whose relaxation alone raised growth, by 627% in air and 78% at elevated CO2. Bottleneck analysis showed that growth is limited by many enzymes spread across the network in both conditions, that the limiting enzymes differ between the two, and that control over starch metabolism seen in air disappears at elevated CO2. Measured proteomes agreed with these predictions, since the predicted bottleneck enzymes were more abundant than other enzymes. Rapid growth in P. celeri therefore reflects how the protein budget is allocated more than how large it is. Therefore, eciPiccel954 provides a quantitative basis for engineering this alga for biotechnological application.

title: Quantum Barcoding Bridges High-Dimensional Immune Phenotyping with Signaling Responses across Species
content: Cross-species immune profiling is limited by marker-panel size and antibody cross-reactivity. We benchmark Quantum Barcoding (QBC), a split-pool oligo-antibody assay, against mass cytometry in human and rhesus macaque blood and integrate separately measured cells using MARIO. The resulting computationally matched profiles carry 174 protein features. Population-frequency concordance was higher in humans (Pearson r = 0.92) than rhesus macaques (r = 0.55), and fusion resolved complementary lineage subsets. Unstimulated signaling conservation varied by lineage, with B-cell profiles correlated across species (Spearman {rho} = 0.70). In the primary PBMC-reference analysis, GM-CSF increased pSTAT5 in human monocytes and dendritic populations and rhesus dendritic cells. Network inference identified convergent pSTAT5-centered connectivity changes in human monocytes and rhesus dendritic cells, including pSTAT1-edge reversal and gained pSTAT3/pERK coupling. These results connect broad surface phenotypes to inferred signaling organization while retaining species- and population-specific differences.

title: A conserved pituitary response to tissue loss controls regeneration across vertebrates
content: Regenerating complex tissues requires coordination between local cellular responses and body-wide systemic signals. As a central endocrine regulator, the pituitary is well positioned to coordinate this process. Here, we identify the pituitary as an injury-responsive regulator of axolotl limb and tilapia fin regeneration. Limb loss triggered sustained transcriptional responses in the axolotl pituitary. Single-cell transcriptomics linked pituitary loss to altered gene expression in prolactin- and growth hormone-responsive limb cells. Local disruption of the prolactin receptor impaired digit formation, whereas combined hormone treatment partially restored regeneration in hypophysectomized axolotls. In tilapia, pituitary removal impaired fin regeneration and prolactin-related signaling. Mouse digits differed from axolotls and tilapia in how and when they received pituitary signals during regeneration, suggesting pituitary-dependent regrowth is evolutionarily divergent among highly regenerative vertebrates.

title: Probing bacterial fitness in virtual chemostats
content: The growth rate of a bacterial population is a fundamental quantity in microbiology, but hard to predict from mechanistic single-cell models. Simulating exponentially growing cell populations is computationally infeasible, and single-lineage estimates are biased as they do not account for phenotypic selection between cells. We present computational algorithms to efficiently estimate growth rates with arbitrary accuracy by combining ideas from branching processes and particle filtering. These can be used with general agent-based cell models at a cost quadratic in the desired accuracy, bypassing the exponential complexity of naive approaches. Applying these methods to single-cell models of Escherichia coli, we study how single-cell heterogeneity in antibiotic responses shapes population dynamics, and how bacterial locomotion and chemotaxis in fluctuating environments affect their long-term growth.

title: Putative biosurfactants from polar microbial consortia
content: Biosurfactants (BS) are amphiphilic microbial metabolites that are biodegradable, low in toxicity, and environmentally compatible, making them attractive for applications in food, pharmaceutical, and bioremediation industries. This study investigated the phylogenetic composition and biosurfactant-producing potential of marine oil snow (MOS)-associated microbial consortia from the Churchill Marine Observatory, western Hudson Bay. MOS aggregates were cultivated in mineral Bushnell-Haas (BH) medium supplemented with 3% (w/v) NaCl, using motor oil as the sole hydrocarbon source. Enrichment cultures capable of growth in BH medium were subsequently evaluated for biosurfactant production using qualitative and quantitative assays at 4 {degrees}C and 20 {degrees}C. All cultures were maintained as enrichment consortia throughout the study. A total of eight enrichment cultures were identified as biosurfactant-producing consortia. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Pseudoalteromonas dominated all consortia, while Paraglaciecola, Marinomonas, and other taxa were present at varying relative abundances. Although none of the consortia exhibited high emulsification activity (E24 > 40%), biosurfactant yields were significantly higher at 4 {degrees}C. Additionally, three consortia tested positive for rhamnolipid-type biosurfactant production.

title: Tandem repeats in methanogenic archaea and their viruses reveal a shared potential for rapid genomic diversification
content: Methanogenic archaea drive global methane emissions, yet the molecular basis of their physiological flexibility is unclear. Archaeal adaptation is typically attributed to horizontal gene transfer, which is episodic and cannot explain rapid, reversible change. Here we show that direct tandem repeats (TRs) offer an intrinsic alternative. By screening 50,567 prokaryotic genomes, we find TR densities in Methanosarcina more than 30-fold above the prokaryotic average, paralleling Borg extrachromosomal elements. These TRs recur at conserved loci while sharing almost no sequence identity between strains, indicating independent origin, and evolve during routine cultivation. Methanogen TRs are transcribed, show ribosome occupancy, and lie near regulatory and cofactor-related genes, whilst being depleted around core energy-conserving and translational machinery. Genic TRs generate intrinsically disordered regions in proteins carrying nucleotide-binding, protein-protein interaction and cell-surface domains, and occur in structural and surface proteins of methanogen-infecting viruses. TRs are therefore an overlooked source of variability and adaptation potential in methanogens and their viruses.

title: DarHTG is a tripartite phage defence system for purine DNA base ADP-ribosylation
content: Bacteria evolved a variety of phage defence strategies to combat the constant onslaught of viral threats. DarTG toxin-antitoxin systems provide phage defence by ADP-ribosylation of bases in single-stranded DNA which interferes with viral replication and aborts phage infection. Here, we describe DarHTG, a system widespread among bacteria, that combines DarTG with a non-processive superfamily I helicase functioning as co-toxin for DarT and thereby enabling the ADP-ribosylation of double-stranded DNA. We identified two such DarHTG subclasses which catalyse the ADP-ribosylation of adenosine and guanosine bases, respectively, and reverse these modifications with structurally unique ARH superfamily antitoxins. Thus, DarHTG antitoxins expand the known macromolecular target spectrum of the ARH enzyme class to nucleic acids. These DarHTG systems confer resistance to a broad range of bacteriophages and can be triggered by the highly charged tails of viral single-stranded DNA-binding proteins, which occlude the active site of the ARH antitoxin.

title: Draft genome of Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 isolated from marine oil snow in the Churchill Marine Observatory, MB, Canada
content: An oil-degrading enrichment culture was inoculated from Marine Oil Snow (MOS) collected during an oil-spill experiment at the Churchill Marine Observatory in winter 2024. The complete metagenome-assembled genome for Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 was reconstructed, exhibiting the genetic potential to degrade hydrocarbons, including alkanes and aromatic compounds, as well as the ability to produce surfactants.

title: Structure of Bacillus cereus ZmaM, a peptidase-ABC transporter that secretes and activates zwittermicin A
content: Bacteria engage in microbial warfare by secreting toxic molecules. These toxins can serve as therapeutics or drug discovery starting points, motivating investigations of their production. Bacteria that produce these toxins must protect themselves, and a common strategy is to synthesize an inactive prodrug that is activated upon secretion. Some prodrugs are capped with N-acyl-[x1D05]-asparagine motifs, which are removed by two types of prodrug peptidases. Type I peptidases are membrane-bound S12 hydrolases; type II peptidases have an additional C-terminal half-ABC transporter module. Recent structures of a type I peptidase revealed how its transmembrane domain completes the substrate-binding site, but little is known about type II peptidases. Here, we show that the B. cereus type II peptidase ZmaM is responsible for both the export of prezwittermicin and its activation into zwittermicin. The structure of homodimeric ZmaM reveals a central type IV ABC transporter flanked by peptidase modules. The periplasmic hydrolase domains interact over the transporter's open outer vestibule. Mutations to intermodule interfaces impact both peptidase and ATP hydrolysis activities, indicating the peptidase and transporter modules are interdependent. Together, our findings reveal an evolutionary strategy to coordinate toxin activation with its export and inform future efforts to harness these systems in biotechnology.

title: Genome-wide CRISPRi-seq maps essential-gene contributions to aminoglycoside susceptibility in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic ESKAPE pathogen whose multiple intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance mechanisms restrict treatment options. Essential genes offer potential antimicrobial targets, but their vulnerability to partial inhibition and contribution to antibiotic susceptibility remain incompletely characterized. Here, we developed a rhamnose-inducible CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) platform and an 83,078-guide library for genome-wide screening in PAO1, with mismatch guides enabling graded repression. Fitness profiling in antibiotic-free Mueller-Hinton medium identified 743 genes whose repression reduced competitive fitness and revealed sequence features associated with guide performance. Combining full-match and mismatch-guide responses revealed substantial variation in essential-gene fitness effects across predicted repression strengths, while comparison of fitness profiles between Mueller-Hinton medium and fetal bovine serum identified condition-dependent effects alongside a conserved fitness landscape. Under aminoglycoside exposure, we identified 118 recurrent sensitizing and 120 recurrent protective gene knockdowns, including many targeting essential and fitness-associated functions. Growth and killing assays with individual strains confirmed that CRISPRi targeting of atpI, accC, secA and ftsZ enhanced tobramycin activity. Finally, transcriptome analysis of these knockdowns confirmed target silencing, captured polar effects on neighboring genes and revealed distinct but overlapping transcriptional responses. Together, these findings quantify the variable fitness costs of essential-gene repression and identify candidate targets for potentiating aminoglycoside activity.

title: CYP123, a sterol C4-methyl oxidase, acts with CYP51 to initiate mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism
content: Mycobacteria exploit host cholesterol, both as a carbon source and as a source of catabolites proposed to modulate host immunity, but their capacity to catabolise other host sterols has not been established. Lanosterol, the first sterol intermediate of host cholesterol biosynthesis, accumulates in the activated macrophages these bacteria infect. Here we define the initiating steps of mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism, combining genomic enzymology, transcriptional profiling, mutagenesis, biochemistry, NMR and crystallography. We identify the cytochrome P450 CYP123 as a sterol C4-methyl oxidase. It is encoded with the lanosterol 14-demethylase CYP51 in a co-oriented region conserved across most Mycobacteriaceae. The region carries no binding site for the cholesterol-responsive regulators KstR or KstR2, and in M. abscessus lanosterol induces both genes while cholesterol does not. CYP123 oxidises the C4-methyl group of C14-demethylated sterols in three steps to the carboxylic acid, yet acts on neither lanosterol nor cholesterol, because Met82 excludes the C14-methylated precursor. An M82A variant binds and oxidises lanosterol. In a single reaction containing both recombinant M. smegmatis enzymes, CYP51 converts lanosterol to FF-MAS, which CYP123 then oxidises to the C4-carboxylic acid, so the two act in sequence. M. smegmatis, M. phlei and M. abscessus grow on lanosterol as a sole carbon source. Growth slows in M. smegmatis cyp123 and cyp51 mutants. Mycobacterial sterol catabolism therefore extends beyond cholesterol, and blocking the cholesterol route alone may not deprive these organisms of host sterols. Induction where lanosterol confers no growth advantage raises the possibility that the pathway also serves functions beyond carbon acquisition.

title: Nanobodies against Plasmodium vivax AMA1 block parasite invasion
content: Plasmodium vivax is the most widespread malaria species to infect human populations. P. vivax invades young red cells called reticulocytes to replicate and proliferate. An essential protein in parasite invasion is the Apical Membrane Antigen 1, PvAMA1, which forms the tight junction between parasite and red cell membrane through its interaction with Rhoptry Neck Protein 2, PvRON2. Here we report the identification of PvAMA1 nanobodies using phage display in combination with Sanger sequencing, next-generation sequencing and structure prediction tools. We show that these nanobodies bind with high affinities and across several different epitopes on PvAMA1. Several nanobodies recognize PvAMA1 in merozoites of late-stage schizonts and inhibit parasite invasion of red blood cells. These growth inhibitory nanobodies bind to conformational epitopes of PvAMA1 and most bind to a site distinct from a known potent human monoclonal antibody 826827. Crystal structures of two inhibitory nanobodies in complex with PvAMA1 show that they bind novel neutralizing epitopes which are outside the hydrophobic groove that contacts PvRON2. Furthermore, we show that two other PvAMA1 nanobodies also inhibit Plasmodium falciparum invasion. These results demonstrate the potential of PvAMA1 nanobodies to inhibit malaria parasite invasion across multiple Plasmodium species.

title: One-step glycan photoaffinity probe synthesis enables identification of human milk oligosaccharide-interacting microbiota
content: Glycans are found on the surfaces of all living cells and engage in cell signaling through the binding of various molecular targets. However, chemical probes to detect and identify carbohydrate interactions remain difficult to produce, due in large part to the challenges of late-stage, site-specific functionalization of oligosaccharides. Here, we report the synthesis and application of a minimal bifunctional diazirine/alkyne linker utilizing an N,O-dialkylhydroxylamine (NODHA) moiety that can readily be installed on the anomeric position of unprotected sugars. Our linker functionalizes glycans with complete {beta}-stereoselectivity, appends less mass than a single hexose unit, and maintains the closed-ring structure of the reducing end sugar. With this molecule, we generate glycan photoaffinity probes in a single step using unprotected human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs). We then validate binding selectivity of our compounds using lectins with known affinity towards our sugars. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these glycan photoaffinity probes by performing photocrosslinking on a complex microbiota community and use cell sorting paired with metagenomic sequencing to identify potential new HMO-interacting microbes. Together, our work provides a one-step route to synthesize photoaffinity probes from unprotected, reducing glycans for interrogating carbohydrate interactions at the host-microbiota interface.

title: Isolation and characterization of diverse Veillonella phages reveal novel lineages and distinct host interactions
content: The human oral microbiome is diverse and home to many species of bacteria, archaea, microeukaryotes, fungi and viruses. Homeostasis in the oral microbiome is important for health and dysbiosis in these communities leads to periodontal and systemic diseases. Veillonella are gram-negative, anaerobic, lactate-fermenting early colonizers of the mouth and are abundant in healthy oral microbiomes. Although considered commensals, Veillonella serve as bridging species in dental biofilms, promoting later colonization by pathogens, with mounting evidence supporting their roles as accessory pathogens in dental caries and periodontal disease. Bacteriophages are key regulators of bacterial community composition and are important drivers of microbial diversity, evolution, and ecology of the oral environment. Despite the ecological importance of Veillonella in the oral microbiome, phages infecting Veillonella remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we report the isolation of ten phages infecting natural isolates of three Veillonella species, representing seven distinct phage genomes. These phages exhibit diverse morphologies, genome organizations, and host ranges, with infection restricted to strains within the species of isolation. Several phages establish stable lysogeny, confer resistance to superinfection, and differ substantially in spontaneous production of infectious phage progeny. Genetic analysis of resistant mutants implicates lipopolysaccharide O-antigen as the receptor for one phage. Although none of the isolated phages had close matches in existing oral virome catalogs, related sequences were detected in oral metagenomes from geographically diverse populations. Together, these findings establish an experimentally characterized collection of Veillonella phages and connect previously uncharacterized oral viral diversity to bacterial hosts and infection phenotypes.

title: Molecular and Structural Characterisation of the MERS-Coronavirus Polymerase
content: MERS-CoV (Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus) belongs to the Betacoronavirus genus, which also includes SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of the COVID-19 pandemic. MERS-CoV is the pathogen responsible for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), a respiratory disease with a 36.5% case fatality rate. Given the capacity of coronaviruses for genetic recombination and mutation, MERS-CoV remains a pathogen of significant pandemic potential, with viral evolution potentially facilitating enhanced adaptation and transmission in humans. There are no approved treatments for MERS-CoV infection. The MERS-CoV replication-transcription complex (RTC), a multimeric protein complex key to genome amplification, has no cellular analogues and a highly conserved sequence, making it a useful target for antiviral compounds; however, structural and biochemical characterisation of the MERS-CoV RTC is limited. Here, we characterise the minimal MERS-CoV RTC using in vitro and single-molecule assays and show that it is susceptible to the RNA-dependent-RNA-polymerase inhibitor suramin. We present a structure of the minimal MERS-CoV RTC in complex with an RNA duplex, which shows strong structural similarity to the SARS-CoV-2 RTC. We use cross-subunit swapping experiments to show that the MERS-CoV NSP12 core can efficiently utilise SARS-CoV-2 cofactors NSP7 and NSP8, whereas SARS-CoV-2 NSP12 exhibits reduced in vitro activity with the MERS-CoV NSP8. This asymmetric cross-species compatibility highlights both the evolutionary conservation and virus-specific adaptation of coronavirus polymerase-cofactor interactions. Together, these findings provide a structural and mechanistic framework for understanding MERS-CoV RNA synthesis and establish its conserved RTC as a potential target for the development of broadly acting coronavirus antivirals.

title: Microbial plankton in southern Hudson Bay and James Bay in late summer
content: Hudson Bay and James Bay, on the southern margin of the Arctic, are warming and freshening as river discharge increases and surrounding permafrost thaws, yet their microbial plankton remain poorly described, and James Bay and the waters around the Belcher Islands have never been surveyed with environmental DNA. We conducted the first dedicated DNA-based survey of eukaryotic and prokaryotic plankton in southern Hudson Bay and James Bay, sequencing 18S rRNA (V9) and 16S rRNA (V4) gene amplicons from 72 samples collected at 51 stations in August 2022 and 2023. Hierarchical clustering resolved nine distinct communities; the primary division separated surface James Bay from Hudson Bay, with further structuring by year, distance to coast, depth, and riverine influence. Temperature, salinity, depth, and distance to coast together explained 31% of community variation (distance-based redundancy analysis), and threshold indicator taxa analysis placed an abrupt community-level change in offshore surface waters at 55.3 N and a salinity of ~24.5. Across this boundary, primary producers shifted from large Chaetoceros diatoms in Hudson Bay to the picoplanktonic green alga Picochlorum and the cyanobacterium Cyanobium in James Bay, while large Gyrodinium dinoflagellates and Calanus copepods gave way to Gymnodinium, Pseudocalanus, and small cercozoans and ciliates. Heterotrophic bacteria in Hudson Bay were dominated by Proteobacteria, Bacteroidota, and Verrucomicrobiota, likely using diatom- and dinoflagellate-derived organic matter, whereas Actinomycetota and Planctomycetota dominated James Bay, likely using cyanobacterial and terrestrial dissolved organic matter. Prokaryotic diversity was highest in riverine, estuarine, and James Bay waters and declined northward and seaward. We also report the first strong presence of marine Synechococcus CC9902 in Hudson Bay and identify cosmopolitan bacteria that provide a baseline for future monitoring. These results suggest that continued freshening of the Hudson Bay Complex will favour smaller primary producers and a stronger microbial loop, and that ecosystem shifts may occur abruptly once surface waters cross a salinity threshold.

title: NAD Metabolism Drives CTCF-Cohesin Chromatin Regulation in EBV-Transformed B-Cells
content: Chromatin architecture regulates gene expression, and it is maintained by architectural proteins such as CTCF and the cohesin complex. In Epstein Barr virus infected cells, viral chromatin organization is stabilized through the interaction between PARP1 and CTCF, ensuring maintenance of latent gene expression. EBV B cells exhibit elevated PARP1 activity, which imposes a substantial metabolic burden due to NAD consumption by PARP1 itself. We demonstrate that efficient EBV infection and B-cell transformation rely on the NAD salvage pathway to sustain PARP1 activity and CTCF and cohesin chromatin folding. Pharmacologic inhibition of the rate-limiting enzyme NAMPT with FK866 phenocopies the chromatin architectural disruption induced by PARP1 and changes in NAD levels affects CTCF/cohesin chromatin architectural remodeling and loop extrusion. Moreover, NAMPT inhibition reduces tumor burden in EBV xenograft models. These findings identify a critical metabolic dependency linking NAD homeostasis to CTCF-cohesin mediated chromatin architecture and reveal a therapeutic vulnerability in EBV-associated malignancies.

title: Therapeutic vulnerabilities of the drug-resistant fungal meningitis pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans
content: Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is FKS1, encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that fks1{triangleup} mutants lack {beta}-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.

title: The ecological niche and seasonality of Theileria equi in Portugal
content: Equine piroplasmosis, caused by the tick-borne protozoan Theileria equi, is an evolving concern in Europe. In recent years, it has been associated with substantial economic costs and with transmission showing signs of pushing into previously free or marginal northern regions. While piroplasmosis is endemic in Portugal, not much is known about the interplay of seasonally varying and spatial abiotic drivers that may modulate infection. In this study, we leveraged unique field-surveillance data based on equine PCR testing together with publicly available data to unravel and characterize the spatio-temporal dynamics and ecological niche of Theileria equi. Infection probability was estimated to increase with local bovine abundance, temperature and the presence of planosol soils, and to decrease with local equine density due to an intraspecific dilution effect of vector exposure. At an individual level, the highest infection probabilities were estimated among female and pasture-kept equids. We estimate strong seasonal signatures in local and national infection probability, maximized in August and minimized in February, and a spatially heterogeneous ecological niche landscape. Far northern and north-eastern regions combined low infection probability both in- and off-season with prolonged off-seasons, whereas centre and north-western regions combined high probability both in- and off-season with brief off-seasons. The former plausibly function as unsuitable reservoirs, and the latter as suitable year-round reservoirs. Our results provide a first quantitative, risk-stratified basis for regional and individual targeted Theileria equi surveillance, awareness and control in Portugal.

title: Species identity rather than colony size partitions shape variation in six Caribbean octocorals
content: Caribbean reefs are increasingly dominated by arborescent octocorals as scleractinian cover declines. The physical structure of these octocoral forests is established by the manner in which octocoral species generate and modify colony form as they grow. We tested whether colony shape exhibited species-specific architecture and whether it changed allometrically with size. Two-dimensional projections of colony form were modeled as a series of stacked bands, whose areas were measured from scaled in situ images of colonies of six sympatric Caribbean octocorals from St John, US Virgin Islands. Principal component analysis (PCA) of relative band areas resolved a single dominant axis, accounting for 67.9% of the variation, that separated top-heavy from bottom-heavy colony profiles. Species identity explained 42% of the total variation in relative form, whereas colony height only explained 2% and had no detectable effect on either PCA axis. The proportion of the colony outline occupied by branches increased with height, from a predicted 41% at 20 cm to 52% at 100 cm. Colonies therefore grew without a detectable redistribution of area along their vertical axis, filling a species-specific outline more densely rather than moving along a common allometric trajectory. The vertical geometry of an octocoral canopy may therefore depend more on which species are present than on the sizes its colonies have reached.

title: Intraspecific trait variation shapes macro-scale patterns ofniche breadth and range size
content: Morphological variation within species may promote adaptation across ecological and geographic space, perhaps reflecting evolutionary plasticity and adaptability. Based on this concept, species with greater intraspecific variation in morphological traits may be expected to occupy broader ecological niches and larger geographic ranges. However, even in the age of global trait datasets, intraspecific morphological variation remains poorly quantified at broad taxonomic and geographic scales, limiting our understanding of how trait flexibility shapes ecological and biogeographic patterns. Focusing on 161 species of bulbuls, a widespread avian family containing some of the most abundant bird species in the world, along with some of the rarest and most restricted in range, we conducted global-scale sampling of morphological traits. These included beak shape, tarsus length and wing length, associated with dietary niche, foraging strategy and dispersal, respectively. Using phylogenetic models, we tested whether ecological niche breadth and geographical range size are predicted by intraspecific morphological variation quantified from 8,251 museum specimens and 5,627 live captures. Our results demonstrate that morphological trait variation predicts both ecological niche breadth and geographic range size. Furthermore, widespread species exhibit greater morphological variation than restricted-range species even when comparisons are constrained to equivalent geographic extents, consistent with the hypothesis that intraspecific trait variation facilitates range expansion rather than simply accumulating as a consequence of occupying a larger range. These results identify intraspecific morphological variation as a potentially important, yet largely overlooked, predictor of ecological traits and biogeographic distributions in birds.

title: Particle-based representation of phytoplankton modulates emergent coexistence and biogeography in a model ocean
content: Phytoplankton communities sustain the marine food web through primary productivity. These communities sustain a high diversity of species, all of which must draw from the same finite nutrient supply. The mechanisms driving phytoplankton biogeography and succession, as well as those enabling high diversity, remain incompletely understood. Here, we compare emerging patterns of biogeography, richness, and diversity in a size-structured phytoplankton community as it is advected and diffused within an idealized North Atlantic double-gyre circulation, using both Eulerian and Lagrangian (particle-based) modeling (PBM) frameworks. When a sufficient number of particles is modeled, the PBM, which resolves mortality at the particle level, produces stronger seasonal variability in biomass in the northern gyre and less stable and higher biomass in the southern gyre, while reproducing large-scale chlorophyll patterns observed by satellite. These contrasting dynamics are accompanied by distinct regional diversity patterns: local richness and diversity are generally higher in the PBM than in the Eulerian model in the northern gyre, with differences depending on the mortality threshold, whereas in the oligotrophic southern gyre, PBM local richness increases with particle number, while Eulerian richness is more sensitive to the mortality threshold. The PBM also produces a dynamic and emergent biogeographical structure that is more robust to the mortality threshold than the Eulerian model. Finally, Lagrangian variability in environmental conditions experienced by particles shows a stronger impact compared to the local Eulerian variability in the Northern gyre and stresses variable sensitivity to environmental histories. Together, these results suggest that the discrete representation of biomass fundamentally alters mortality, biogeography, and emergent coexistence patterns in model plankton ecosystems.

title: Interactive effects of Nutrient Enrichment and Water Scarcity on Floral signaling and visitation
content: - Floral traits remain an underexplored frontier in global change biology compared to their vegetative counterparts. As anthropogenic change involves simultaneous shifts in resource availability, focusing on isolated stressors may overlook complex biological responses. Characterizing the interactive effects of these stressors is therefore crucial to move beyond additive models and accurately predict the stability of pollination services in a transforming world. - The individual and interactive effects of nutrient enrichment and water scarcity were investigated on the floral traits and pollinator visitation rates of five grassland species. - While species identity emerged as the dominant driver of overall trait variation, across-species responses were also present. Among the abiotic drivers, nutrient enrichment emerged as the primary influence, significantly increasing flower number and achromatic contrast while decreasing floral area, chromatic contrast and chroma. Conversely, water scarcity primarily reduced plant height and increased floral chroma and hue. The two factors also often interacted in their effects. The changes in visual traits scaled up to changes in pollinator visitation, but the specific effects were largely species-specific. - Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that anthropogenic stressors act in divergent ways to reshape floral phenotypes and pollinator visitation, advancing our understanding of plant-pollinator interactions under compounding global pressures.

title: Concrete waste as a source of calcium and alkalinity for coccolithophore cultivation: an experimental test of carbon dioxide removal and sequestration
content: Cultivation of calcifying microalgae has been proposed as a route to carbon dioxide removal (CDR), but biogenic calcification releases CO2 unless the calcium supplied also adds alkalinity. We used cultures of the coccolithophore Chrysotila sp to test whether hydrated lime (Ca(OH)2), supplied as a reagent or within ground waste concrete, can provide both calcium and alkalinity. In a 26-day factorial batch experiment, we monitored pH, nitrate and dissolved calcium. Calcite was quantified by thermogravimetric analysis. Nitrate concentration decreased and calcite accumulated in all algal treatments, indicating that lime or concrete did not inhibit growth or calcification. Lime and concrete raised culture pH significantly whereas the algal growth rate inferred from nitrate drawdown did not differ among treatments. Calcite production was 3.6-fold higher with lime than in seawater (4.5 vs. 1.2 mg L-1 d-1) and highly variable with concrete; lime and concrete cultures remained supersaturated with respect to calcite ({Omega} {approx} 7-10 vs. 0.2). Carbonate-system calculations indicate that the added alkalinity raises the equilibrium CO2 uptake capacity of the medium by ca. 3.4 mmol kg-1, offsetting CO2 released by calcification. These results provide proof of concept for coupling coccolithophore cultivation with concrete waste reuse for CDR.

title: Combined elevated temperature and CO2 alter Wolbachia abundance and host fitness but not cytoplasmic incompatibility in a stored-product pest
content: Coinfecting endosymbiont strains may respond differently to environmental change, with consequences for host performance and reproductive incompatibility. We investigated an isofemale line of Callosobruchus chinensis coinfected with the cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI)-inducing Wolbachia strains wBruCon (Con) and wBruOri (Ori), together with derived Con-only and uninfected sublines. Beetles were maintained under control conditions (30{degrees}C, ~500 ppm CO2) or under combined elevated temperature and CO2 (32{degrees}C, ~1000 ppm CO2; eT&CO2). In coinfected adults, Ori relative abundance declined under eT&CO2, whereas Con abundance increased in females. Con responses also depended on host sex and infection status, with singly infected males showing particularly high abundance under control conditions. However, CI expression remained stable across environmental conditions. Coinfected females laid fewer eggs than uninfected females, whereas host life-history responses to eT&CO2 varied among traits and generations. eT&CO2 accelerated development and reduced adult longevity, while reduced egg-adult survival emerged in the F2 generation. It also reduced F1 fecundity but only in the uninfected subline. Strong and partial CI associated with Con and Ori, respectively, remained evident under both environmental conditions. Equilibrium analyses incorporating relative fecundity, CI intensity, and maternal transmission suggested lower infection persistence under eT&CO2 in the F1 generation but higher persistence in the F2 generation. Sensitivity analysis suggested contribution of improved relative fecundity of infected females in the latter. Overall, the two Wolbachia strains exhibited contrasting, sex-dependent abundance responses to eT&CO2, while CI expression remained stable. These findings suggest that climate change may alter symbiont infection dynamics in economically important pests, with potential implications for symbiont-mediated traits, including pesticide resistance.

title: Transcriptomic Signatures Suggest Epigenetic Programming of Molecular Defense in Biochar-Exposed Formica japonica
content: Previous transcriptomic analyses revealed that exposing the ant species Formica japonica to biochar induces a priming effect that is sustained under heavy metal stress and enhances the ants' resilience. Re-evaluation of the data shows that biochar exposure acts as an epigenetic switch, programming the ants' defense mechanisms and enhancing their resilience to various environmental stressors. Exposure to humic-like substances, such as biochar leachate, prepares insects to withstand not only heavy metals but also other environmental challenges, such as exposure to xenobiotics, pathogens, and parasites.

title: Directed evolution and characterisation of light harvesting complexes with altered spectral properties in purple non-sulfur bacteria
content:
Abstract
Purple non-sulfur bacteria (PNSB) are metabolically versatile microorganisms that inhabit diverse environments taking advantage of a remarkably efficient photosynthetic machinery. In this work, we describe the creation of a workflow for experimental studies aiming to compare the light absorption properties of structural variants of the light-harvesting complex 2 (LH2) of PNSB. Through the creation of a library of LH2 variants using site-directed mutagenesis, we engineered proteins with different spectral properties to be expressed in a LH2-defficient mutant of the model PNSB Rhodobacter sphaeroides. We validated this approach by reproducing a previously described mutant with a blue-shift in the B850 absorption peak, in addition to identifying a novel mutant exhibiting a red-shift of this peak. We characterised the fluorescence lifetime of the purified LH2 spectral variants in vitro. Our results suggest that directed evolution approaches can be used to systematically explore the landscape of light absorption in LH2s variants.

title: Simulating Science Communication for Vulnerable Populations: A Project-Based Learning Exercise in Undergraduate Medical Microbiology
content:
Abstract
While undergraduate medical education relies heavily on traditional lectures to deliver foundational biomedical sciences, standard models frequently isolate pathogens and mechanisms from the socio-economic realities of healthcare and community communication. To address this gap, we implemented and evaluated a project-based active learning intervention conducted in a classroom setting in a Medical Microbiology course, challenging students to synthesize complex scientific literature and design educational brochures tailored for socially vulnerable populations. At the end of the academic semester, student perceptions were evaluated through an anonymous mixed-methods survey completed by 51 participants. The quantitative outcomes revealed high student satisfaction, with participants perceiving the instructions as highly transparent and the cognitive challenge as well-balanced. Notably, most of the students reported that the project successfully consolidated core microbiological content, while also stating that focusing on vulnerable communities significantly expanded their understanding of how social determinants impact infectious diseases. This strong positive feedback was also present in the thematic analysis of the open-ended responses, which showed that students highly valued practicing the translation of technical medical jargon into accessible, community-friendly language within this simulated exercise, which was conducted among peers and instructors. The primary challenges reported were operational, centered on group coordination and managing the heavy academic workload typical of the end of the semester. Overall, our findings suggest that integrating brochure design and public health context into the basic science curriculum effectively anchors microbiology to clinical and humanistic realities, fostering preliminary communication skills, teamwork, and social responsibility better than standard expository lessons.

title: Flagella‐Mediated Biofilm Formation and 3D Swarming Drive Virulence in the Honey Bee Pathogen Paenibacillus larvae
content:
The flagella of the bacterial pathogen Paenibacillus larvae, the etiological agent of American foulbrood in honey bees, were characterized and identified as virulence factors. These cellular appendages play key roles in biofilm formation and 3D swarming, two multicellular behaviours of P. larvae that contribute to pathogenesis.

ABSTRACT
American foulbrood, a devastating bacterial disease affecting honey bee larvae, represents a major threat to apiculture worldwide. Its etiological agent, the Gram‐positive, endospore‐forming bacterium Paenibacillus larvae, has therefore been extensively studied to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying its pathogenicity and to identify key virulence determinants. In the present study, we identified the peritrichous flagella of P. larvae as a novel and important virulence factor of the genotype ERIC II. A flagella‐deficient mutant was generated and shown to exhibit multiple defects in vitro associated with biofilm formation, including altered biofilm architecture, reduced adhesion, impaired floating capacity and loss of swarming motility. Survival assays using honey bee larvae, complemented by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analyses of infected larvae, further demonstrated the crucial contribution of flagella to virulence in vivo by mediating biofilm formation on the larval midgut epithelium as well as three‐dimensional swarming during epithelial invasion.

title: Enhanced weathering of glacial rock flour drives coupled inorganic and organic carbon sequestration in a five-year field experiment

Enhanced weathering of glacial rock flour drives coupled inorganic and organic carbon sequestration in a five-year field experiment
Christiana Dietzen, Malgorzata Rizzi, Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, and Minik Thorleif Rosing
Biogeosciences, 23, 7727–7742, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7727-2026, 2026
Enhanced rock weathering involves spreading ground silicate rock on farmland to remove atmospheric CO₂ as the rock dissolves. Soil samples taken five years after Greenlandic glacial rock flour was applied to a Danish field showed that over half the applied material had dissolved, yet the increase in soil organic carbon was substantially greater than the estimated inorganic carbon uptake through weathering. This highlights the importance of considering both pathways when assessing climate impact.

title: Contrasting Responses of Carbon Dioxide and Methane Fluxes Following Thermokarst Erosion Across Tundra‐Lake Interfaces in the Western Canadian Arctic
content:
Abstract
Erosion from ice‐rich permafrost thaw (“thermokarst”) alters tundra vegetation cover and soil moisture, and laterally transports organic material into lakes, altering net fluxes of carbon dioxide (FCO2), methane (FCH4), and nitrous oxide (FN2O). Tundra and lakes are rarely examined together, although a joint view is necessary to understand their coupled biogeochemical responses to widespread thermokarst erosion. We aimed to understand the impact of thermokarst erosion on FCO2, FCH4 and FN2O and their underlying biogeochemical controls across the tundra‐lake interface. We conducted weekly plot‐scale measurements during the growing season (June–August 2022 and 2023) in stable and eroding tundra and adjacent lakes in the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, NT, Canada. Counterintuitively, eroding tundra absorbed more CO2 than stable tundra (−64.0 ± 79.7 mg C m−2 h−1, n = 85, vs. −26.7 ± 84.2 mg C m−2 h−1, n = 98; mean ± standard deviation), driven by increased photosynthetic activity and higher soil moisture in vegetated eroding tundra. Stable tundra was a net CH4 sink (−0.024 ± 0.027 mg C m−2 h−1, n = 108). This sink capacity increased with an increase in temperature and deepening frost table, but decreased with erosion. Lake FCH4 was significantly higher from eroding lake shores (2.56 ± 5.65 mg C m−2 h−1, n = 88) compared to stable lake shores (1.05 ± 3.61 mg C m−2 h−1, n = 90). Tundra and lake FN2O were generally negligible. The contrasting responses of CO2 and CH4 fluxes highlight the complex effects of thermokarst erosion across the tundra‐lake continuum.

title: Regional Pathways and Impacts of Greenland Ice Sheet Meltwater Simulated in a Sea Ice‒Ocean Model
content:
Abstract
Much attention has been paid to the recent increase in freshwater supply from the Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS). We conducted numerical experiments using a sea ice–ocean model with a nominal 0.25° resolution to investigate pathways of GrIS meltwater and its effects on the surrounding sea‐ice and ocean fields. We first assessed the simulated sea‐ice and ocean fields against available observations to characterize the model's performance and limitations. Within these limitations, the computationally tractable model configuration enabled 30‐year passive tracer experiments for six regional meltwater sources. The total meltwater tracer shows that GrIS meltwater is concentrated in coastal currents around Greenland and subsequently spreads over Baffin Bay. Consistent with previous studies, the meltwater is transported southward by the Labrador Current and is subsequently advected by the North Atlantic Current to the eastern North Atlantic and eventually to the Arctic Ocean. Regional tracers reveal distinct source‐dependent pathways. Meltwater originating from eastern Greenland is transported through the Labrador Sea and across the North Atlantic, eventually reaching the Barents Sea within 20–30 years, whereas meltwater from western Greenland remains largely confined to Baffin Bay and adjacent waters. Comparisons of numerical experiments with and without GrIS meltwater indicate that the meltwater enhances regional ocean stratification and delays sea‐ice melting in the surrounding areas. GrIS meltwater locally increases the alongshore velocity of coastal surface currents by up to 10%. These results highlight the importance of meltwater source location for its decadal redistribution and clarify the regional ocean and sea‐ice responses to GrIS freshwater input.

title: Genetic Novelty and Short‐Term Evolutionary Dynamics in Drosophila yakuba mayottensis
content:
ABSTRACT
Understanding how genetic novelty arises and contributes to population divergence is central to evolutionary biology. On short evolutionary timescales, the relative roles of new mutations and standing variation remain underexplored among structural variation. Here, we compare the contributions of chromosomal rearrangements, tandem duplications and single‐nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to early genomic differentiation in a recently colonized island population, Drosophila yakuba mayottensis, from the island of Mayotte. By comparing the relative impacts of these mutation classes, along with the involvement of transposable elements (TEs), we assess whether certain mutations are more likely to contribute to rapid divergence. We show that TEs are disproportionately involved in the formation of novel structural variants shortly after colonization, particularly through direct insertions. Our results suggest that TE‐associated rearrangements may bypass the clocklike pace of SNP accumulation and divergence, where the contributions of coding SNPs, tandem duplications and TE‐facilitated ectopic recombination are constrained to standing variation on short timescales. Although TEs can drive the rapid emergence of novel variants, their full contribution to adaptation likely depends on evolutionary context and time since colonization. Together, our findings reveal time‐dependent mutational dynamics and highlight the importance of structural variation, particularly TE‐associated rearrangements, in shaping early genomic divergence following habitat shifts.

title: Dating the Colonisation and Source of Adaptive Genetic Variation in the Iago Sparrow (Passer iagoensis)
content:
ABSTRACT
Ancestral adaptive variation is thought to play an important role in facilitating adaptation to insular environments. However, to properly evaluate its role, we need to determine the age of genetic variation. In this study, we investigate the Iago sparrow (Passer iagoensis), a generalist endemic to the Cabo Verde archipelago, to understand how genetic diversity is maintained in an island lineage where populations are likely ephemeral and adaptation to environmental extremes is ongoing. Using whole‐genome sequencing and phenotypic data, we inferred the species' evolutionary history, population structure, and signatures of selection. Our results show that the Iago sparrow diverged from its closest mainland relative approximately 4.26 million years ago, although the colonisation likely occurred only around 2 million years ago. Population structure analyses reveal three distinct lineages, corresponding to geographic divisions within the archipelago, with the Rombos islets population exhibiting significant phenotypic divergence, particularly in bill morphology. Genome scans and phenotypic measurements identified signatures of divergent selection in genes associated with bill size (HMG20B) and bill shape (ALX1), suggesting adaptive evolution in response to local environmental conditions. Our ancestral recombination graph analysis provided temporal estimates for adaptive variation associated with these genes, suggesting that adaptive haplotypes observed in the Rombos population arose after colonisation of the archipelago. This contrasts with patterns described in Darwin's finches, where ancestral variation likely originated prior to colonisation. Our findings highlight the interplay of genetic drift, gene flow, and selection in shaping island species' genetic diversity. The Iago sparrow, a generalist thriving across diverse habitats, provides insights into the mechanisms that maintain genetic diversity in island lineages despite small population sizes and pronounced environmental heterogeneity.

title: Issue Information
Reduction of Tree Water Stress by Large Herbivores in an African Savanna
content:
Using a long‐term herbivore exclusion experiment across a rainfall gradient, we found that excluding large mammals increased savanna tree growth but elevated water stress. Tree sensitivity to exclusion varied among species with contrasting water‐use strategies, indicating that physiological responses may drive shifts in tree communities under altered herbivore and rainfall regimes.

ABSTRACT
Large mammalian herbivores (LMH) play complex roles in shaping tree cover and composition in savannas by suppressing trees through browsing and reducing competition from neighbouring trees and understory vegetation. Where LMH are declining, release from browsing and intensification of competition has unpredictable physiological consequences. To test how LMH removal affects tree growth and water stress, we combined 16 years of growth data with measurements of leaf water potential and gas exchange from a herbivore‐exclusion experiment in Kenya. Across tree species, LMH exclusion increased growth but elevated water stress, particularly under dry conditions. Moreover, the tree species with the most acquisitive water‐use strategy was most susceptible to increased water stress and reduced carbon assimilation under exclusion. These findings indicate that although LMH limit tree growth, they also reduce water stress. Ultimately, interspecific differences in tree physiology will affect how savanna communities respond to interacting pressures from climate change and LMH declines.

title: Is relative risk perpetuating human–wildlife conflicts?
Shapley fields reveal mosaic chemotopic organization in the mouse Olfactory bulb across diverse chemical feature sets
content:
by Nikola Milićević, Shawn D. Burton, Matt Wachowiak, Vladimir Itskov

Neural representations in the olfactory bulb (OB) remain poorly understood compared to well-established coding principles in other sensory systems. This difficulty arises because a natural coordinate system for olfactory stimulus space has not yet been identified, complicating the characterization of neural receptive fields analogous to those in other sensory modalities. Moreover, the extent to which these tuning properties are spatially organized within the OB remains unclear. To advance our understanding of the olfactory coding, we introduce an interpretable method of Shapley fields, as an olfactory analog of retinotopic receptive fields. Shapley fields are spatial distributions of chemical feature importance for the tuning of OB glomeruli. We used this tool to investigate chemotopy in the OB with diverse sets of chemical features using widefield epifluorescence recordings of the mouse dorsal OB in response to stimuli across a wide range of the chemical space. We found that Shapley fields reveal a weak chemotopic organization of the chemical feature sensitivity of dorsal OB glomeruli. This organization was consistent across animals and mostly agreed across very different chemical feature sets: (i) the expert-curated PubChem database features and (ii) features derived from a Graph Neural Network trained on human olfactory perceptual tasks. This chemotopy involved at least three chemical feature dimensions, rather than one or two dominant properties. Moreover, we found that the principal components of the Shapley fields corresponded to single commonly accepted chemical classification groups. This implies that these chemical groups could have been identified purely from the mouse olfactory responses. Our findings suggest that Shapley fields may serve as a chemical feature-agnostic method for investigating olfactory perception.

title: Bayesian efficient coding
content:
by Il Memming Park, Jonathan W. Pillow

The efficient coding hypothesis, which proposes that neurons are optimized to maximize information about the environment, has provided a guiding theoretical framework for sensory and systems neuroscience. More recently, a theory known as the Bayesian Brain hypothesis has focused on the brain’s ability to integrate sensory and prior sources of information in order to perform Bayesian inference. Although pieces of a connection between these two hypotheses have appeared in prior work, a general formulation that treats the optimality criterion as an arbitrary functional of the posterior distribution – and thereby admits both information-based and other objectives within a single framework – has remained largely implicit. Here we make this formulation explicit, developing a Bayesian theory of efficient coding that defines Bayesian efficient codes in terms of four basic ingredients: (1) a stimulus prior distribution; (2) an encoding model; (3) a capacity constraint, specifying a neural resource limit; and (4) a loss functional, quantifying the desirability or undesirability of various posterior distributions. Classic efficient codes arise as the special case in which the loss functional is the posterior entropy, leading to a code that maximizes mutual information, but alternate loss functionals give solutions that differ dramatically from information-maximizing codes. Within this framework we introduce covtropy, a novel family of losses defined on posterior distributions and parameterized by a single exponent, and use it to show that decorrelation of sensory inputs – optimal under classic efficient codes in low-noise settings – can be disadvantageous for objectives that penalize large errors. We then reanalyze Laughlin’s seminal data on contrast coding in the blowfly large monopolar cell, and find that the measured response nonlinearity is better explained by minimizing Lp reconstruction error with p = 1/2 than by information maximization, overturning a forty-year-old interpretation. Bayesian efficient coding thus enlarges the family of codes that are optimal under different objectives and provides a more general framework for understanding the design principles of sensory systems.

title: Saccadic suppression enhances saliency of ecologically relevant stimuli in the zebrafish optic tectum
content:
by Giulia Soto, Carina Thomas, Louis Funk, Tim C. Hladnik, Florian A. Dehmelt, Ziad M. Hafed, Aristides B. Arrenberg

Saccadic suppression, a reduction in visual sensitivity around the time of rapid eye movements, is well-documented in primate psychophysics, but its mechanisms and functions remain debated. Here, we use zebrafish to trace the origins of saccadic suppression, and we demonstrate how saccadic suppression selectively enhances the visual salience of ecologically relevant stimuli. Saccadic suppression thus contributes to more than just compensation for rapid saccade-induced image shifts. We first established a behavioral correlate of saccadic suppression in larval zebrafish escape behavior. Then, using electrophysiology, we show that retinal ganglion cells jumpstart saccadic suppression in a spatial frequency-dependent manner. Calcium imaging, combined with 360° visual stimulation and behavioral tracking, revealed that motor signals enhance peri-saccadic suppression strength in the optic tectum, where suppression lasts for more than 3,000 ms. Notably, saccadic suppression is much weaker and more short-lived for stimuli related to hunting or escape behavior than for behaviorally less relevant global flashes. This unequal attenuation effectively increases the salience of the ecologically relevant stimuli in the optic tectum after saccades. Our results demonstrate that saccadic suppression integrates visual and motor signals to optimize sensory processing within neural constraints, and they provide insights into evolutionarily conserved visual strategies.

title: Recent Slowing Arctic‐Amplified Warming Drives an Unprecedented Water Recovery in the World's Most Voluminous Freshwater Lake
content:
Abstract
The Lake Baikal, containing one‐fifth of Earth's unfrozen surface freshwater, faces increasing hydrological uncertainty under climate change. Its water balance depends on Selenga River inflow and Angara River outflow. We present a 343‐year combined Selenga and Angara streamflow reconstruction using a tree‐ring network to provide a multi‐century hydroclimatic baseline. The reconstruction captures intermittent drying trends throughout the 20th century, including a ∼90% streamflow decline from high levels, consistent with long‐term regional aridification. This trend has reversed sharply over the last decade showing a most sustained ∼80% increase. The recent hydrological recovery is consistent with basin‐wide vegetation greening, rising lake levels, and favorable eco‐climatic conditions, primarily improved water availability. Rapidly changing atmospheric circulations associated with a regional slowing Arctic‐amplified warming drive enhanced moisture transports. The contrasting trend between recent recovery and preceding long‐term decline underscores the need for adaptive management strategies to account for non‐stationary dynamics in safeguarding critical freshwater resources.

title: Iceberg‐Generated Waves From SWOT: Disintegration of Iceberg A‐76A in the Southern Ocean
content:
Abstract
Amid rising global temperatures, icebergs are calving more often and drifting into open waters. Their disintegration processes can trigger energetic surface gravity waves that propagate away from the iceberg remain poorly documented. This study presents an analysis of 12 iceberg‐generated wave fields associated with the disintegration of iceberg A‐76A, utilizing sea surface height anomaly data from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission. We analyzed wave height, wavelength, depth regime, and Time Since Impact (TSI) using wavelet scalograms matched to dispersion curves. Waves fell within the linear intermediate‐to‐deep‐water regime, aligning with findings from Heller et al. (2019, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598‐018‐36634‐3). Correlation found between steepness and TSI, as expected from theory. Preliminary results suggest the potential to infer calving mechanisms and direction from the scalograms. Despite SWOT's limited temporal resolution, demonstrates its unique ability to detect iceberg‐generated and novel view iceberg–ocean interactions, supporting future research with enhanced data and processing capabilities.

title: Aircraft Icing: In‐Cloud Measurements and Explicit Prediction of Supercooled Large Droplets in Icing Clouds of Eastern China Using Multi‐Moment Microphysics Schemes
content:
Abstract
The characteristics of supercooled liquid water (SLW) within icing clouds over eastern China are investigated using in situ aircraft observations and numerical simulations. Supercooled liquid water content increases from 0 to −4°C, but decreases sharply below −4°C. Abundant supercooled large droplets (SLD) were observed, with the effective diameter reaching 175 μm ${\upmu }\mathrm{m}$ and number concentration (Nt) exceeding 19 cm−3. An aircraft icing rate and intensity forecast algorithm is proposed by incorporating flight conditions and SLW spectral characteristics, together with a new diagnostic relation between cloud droplet shape parameter and Nt implemented into the three‐moment NSSL scheme. Sensitivity simulations indicate that the improved scheme can reproduce well the temperature‐dependent variation of SLW content, and significantly enhance forecasted rate of icing, intensity, and icing cloud layer depth.

title: Specialized SWOT SSH Data Assimilation Improves the Representation of Multiscale Variability in the Ocean Model
content:
Abstract
The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission provides wide‐swath sea surface height (SSH) observations at scales poorly sampled by conventional altimetry. Assimilating SWOT data remains challenging because part of the short‐wavelength variance may not be dynamically representable by a given model configuration. We therefore develop a two‐step multiscale 4DVAR framework to assimilate real SWOT SSH observations. The first step constrains broad‐scale SSH mismatches, whereas the second assimilates the remaining SWOT information using a shorter decorrelation scale and the first‐step analysis as background. In the northern South China Sea, the multiscale framework reduces SWOT SSH residuals, yields more organized scale‐dependent increments, and improves the representation and forecast persistence of model‐resolved multiscale SSH variability. Independent SST, Argo, and drifter observations further indicate reduced upper‐ocean thermal biases, mainly within the mixed layer. These results demonstrate that scale‐dependent assimilation can make more effective use of SWOT's multiscale information within a finite‐resolution regional model.

title: Persistence and Dynamics of an Sq‐like Mid‐Latitude Current Vortex During the May 2024 Superstorm
content:
Abstract
The solar quiet (Sq) current system describes the mid‐latitude equivalent current under quiet geomagnetic conditions, but whether an Sq‐like vortex persists during intense storms remains unclear. Using dense East Asian magnetometer observations, including the Chinese Meridian Project, we reconstruct the storm‐time ionospheric equivalent‐current system during the May 2024 superstorm. Observations reveal a persistent Sq‐like mid‐latitude vortex with enhanced intensity and rapid focus displacement. Its evolution follows the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) Bz and couples closely with auroral and equatorial currents. Southward IMF Bz enhances magnetospheric convection, driving auroral‐oval expansion and equatorial electrojet intensification that compress the vortex equatorward, whereas northward turnings lead to auroral retreat and counter‐electrojet pulses, which in turn drive the poleward rebound of the mid‐latitude vortex. Our results extend the Tsuji's model by resolving the mid‐latitude vortex, thereby completing the ionospheric current response chain from auroral currents to the Cowling‐enhanced equatorial response.

title: Asynchronous timing of hypoxia and thermal stress induces diel vertical movement
content:
Abstract
In heterogeneous landscapes, mobile organisms can track habitat conditions across multiple spatial and temporal scales, but selecting one condition often comes at the expense of another. In aquatic ecosystems, trade‐offs between temperature and dissolved oxygen (DO) are ubiquitous, and diel cycles of solar heating and photosynthesis can make them dynamic. Heat stress and hypoxia often occur asynchronously because temperature maximums occur in the evening and oxygen minimums occur around dawn. A key question is whether animal behavior can soften temperature–oxygen trade‐offs by exploiting this asynchrony. We tested how fish respond to diel variation in DO and temperature within vertically stratified thermal refuges. We first monitored heterogeneity in habitat conditions to quantify diel variation in temperature–DO trade‐offs. We then simulated fish depth selection under three strategies: minimizing temperature, maximizing DO, or balancing both variables. Simulations used observed temperature and DO to model depth selection. We then evaluated fish behavior by tagging cutthroat trout with temperature loggers and monitoring their vertical habitat use within enclosures instrumented with temperature–DO sensors. Simulations showed that temperature‐minimizing or oxygen‐maximizing strategies resulted in constant depth selection, whereas fish that balanced temperature and oxygen exhibited diel vertical movement. Most fish exhibited diel vertical movement that matched simulation; however, the movement extent was smaller than expected as fish endured hypoxic conditions in exchange for colder temperatures. We show that diel vertical movement exploits temperature and oxygen asynchrony to soften the trade‐off between these variables. These findings likely apply to other aquatic systems where asynchronous stressors constrain habitat use.

title: Stoichiometric imbalance affects competitive superiority in marine herbivorous zooplankton communities
content:
Abstract
Traditionally, abiotic drivers and predator–prey interactions have been considered critical to shaping the taxonomic composition of a marine zooplankton community, whereas the role of indirect biotic processes, such as exploitative competition, remains unexamined. The competitive performance of a zooplankton taxon can be limited by biochemical mismatches between its requirements and available prey, known as stoichiometric imbalance. Such imbalance impairs zooplankton growth and reproduction, thereby reducing their competitiveness. Stoichiometric imbalance is known to shape zooplankton communities in freshwater systems; however, its role in marine systems has largely been examined only at the species or individual levels under experimental conditions. To fill this gap, we measured the family‐level taxonomic composition and carbon : nitrogen : phosphorus ratios (C : N : P) of herbivorous zooplankton and quantified their stoichiometric imbalance relative to their prey in the southern East China Sea. We examined three hypotheses: Hypothesis 1—Intra‐family stoichiometry of zooplankton is independent of and less variable than phytoplankton; Hypothesis 2—Zooplankton show interfamily variation in stoichiometry; and Hypothesis 3—A higher degree of stoichiometric imbalance reduces the relative abundance of a zooplankton family in the community. Our results showed zooplankton stoichiometry was stable within but variable among families. Family‐level relative abundance was significantly associated with phosphorus imbalance. Despite seasonal shifts in dominant families, the negative relationship between stoichiometric imbalance and relative abundance remained consistent, suggesting that stoichiometric imbalance is an important factor modulating zooplankton community composition across seasons. Notably, phosphorus excess did not negatively affect relative abundance, a pattern that contrasts with the traditional stoichiometric knife‐edge hypothesis.
